patient.title: Pembrolizumab 200 mg · every 3 weeks · lung cancer
patient.purpose: For metastatic lung cancer, the aim is to control cancer and help people live longer. After surgery and platinum chemotherapy, the adjuvant aim is to reduce the chance of cancer returning. Ask which aim applies to you.
patient.context_label: Lung cancer only: first-line metastatic NSCLC or adjuvant NSCLC after surgery and platinum chemotherapy
patient.indication_text: First-line metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer with PD-L1 TPS at least 50% and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation; or adjuvant NSCLC at high risk of recurrence after complete resection and platinum chemotherapy. These are separate uses with different entry criteria and duration.
patient.schedule_summary: Pembrolizumab 200 mg is given as a drip over about 30 minutes on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). The hospital visit is longer because of checks and preparation. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, the adjuvant course lasts up to 12 months. For metastatic cancer, treatment continues while it remains helpful and tolerable; the team may consider stopping after 24 months of sustained response without progression, or continuing when appropriate.
patient.administration_text: An intravenous infusion lasting about 30 minutes, on Day 1 every 3 weeks. Your team chooses suitable venous access and observes for reactions.
patient.monitoring_summary: Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose before every 3-week cycle; thyroid every 3–6 weeks, cortisol if indicated, and symptom review throughout and after treatment.

agents.name: Pembrolizumab
agents.explanation: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.
agents.watch: Report new breathing, bowel, skin, hormone, heart or nerve symptoms promptly; these may be immune inflammation.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, hormone glands, skin, heart and nervous system
Some effects need steroids, hospital care or long-term hormone replacement
Effects may start after the final dose

For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

day_groups.title: Your infusion visit
day_groups.body: The team reviews your blood results, symptoms and medicines. Tell the nurse straight away about itching, flushing, a tight chest, dizziness or feeling suddenly unwell during the drip.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm the next tests, treatment visit and urgent contact number.

day_groups.title: Between visits
day_groups.body: You may feel well between infusions, but immune inflammation can begin at any time. Keep a short symptom record and take medicines exactly as prescribed. Contact your team about new symptoms instead of waiting for your next appointment.
day_groups.action: Confirm thyroid tests are booked every 3–6 weeks, even if infusions are six weeks apart.

support.title: Sickness medicines
support.text: Pembrolizumab alone has a minimal risk of causing sickness. Routine anti-sickness medicines or infusion premedicines are not usually needed; your team can prescribe symptom relief if required.

support.title: Immune alert card
support.text: Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

support.title: Hormones and steroids
support.text: Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines.

support.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least four months after the last dose. If pregnancy is possible or occurs, contact your oncology team promptly.

questions.q: Is my treatment for metastatic cancer or to reduce recurrence after surgery?
questions.a: Ask your team to write down the treatment aim. For metastatic disease, the aim is usually cancer control, symptom relief and more time. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence.

questions.q: Which tumour-test results support this plan?
questions.a: For the first-line metastatic monotherapy pathway, the source requires high PD-L1 expression and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. The adjuvant pathway has different eligibility. Ask which results apply to your own cancer.

questions.q: How long is my course, and what could change it?
questions.a: The adjuvant course lasts up to 12 months. Metastatic treatment continues while helpful and tolerable; a 24-month review may lead to stopping or continuing. Symptoms, response and your preferences can change the plan.

questions.q: Who arranges blood and thyroid tests between visits?
questions.a: The oncology team arranges and reviews tests. Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle; thyroid tests are usually every 3–6 weeks. Ask whether an extra test is needed between six-weekly infusions.

questions.q: Which symptoms should I report straight away, and whom do I contact out of hours?
questions.a: Report new or worsening breathing problems, persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, thirst or a spreading rash promptly. Keep the local oncology and out-of-hours numbers available; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs 112 / 999.

questions.q: What are my alternatives if I choose not to have this treatment?
questions.a: Ask about alternatives for your exact stage and tumour results, including other anticancer treatments, trials, surveillance where appropriate and symptom-focused care. Supportive care remains available whether or not you proceed.

patient.scope_note: This patient suite covers the two lung indications described here. The shared clinical protocol also lists other cancers, which need their own patient information.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be offered
evidence.intro: For suitable people with metastatic lung cancer and a high PD-L1 result, pembrolizumab helped people live longer than chemotherapy in a trial. After surgery and chemotherapy, a separate trial showed a lower risk of recurrence or death; longer-term overall survival was still uncertain at the reported analysis.
evidence.interpretation: These results describe groups of people, not what will happen to one person. The metastatic and after-surgery studies answer different questions.
evidence.population: Two separate lung settings: untreated metastatic PD-L1-high NSCLC; and resected NSCLC at high recurrence risk after chemotherapy.
evidence.limitations: These lung trials used pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks. Trial treatment limits and research scan schedules are not automatic NCCP prescribing rules.

chapters.title: Your lung cancer and treatment aim
chapters.intro: First confirm which lung setting applies to you.

items.title: Metastatic treatment
items.text: Metastatic means the cancer has spread. First-line means the first medicine treatment for this stage. Here, pembrolizumab alone is offered for suitable cancers with a high PD-L1 result and without EGFR or ALK alterations. The aim is usually control, symptom relief and more time.

items.title: After surgery
items.text: Adjuvant means treatment after surgery to reduce the chance of cancer returning. This pathway follows complete resection and platinum chemotherapy for cancer at high risk of recurrence. It does not use the same high PD-L1 requirement as the metastatic pathway.

items.title: Your alternatives
items.text: Ask which other treatments, clinical trials, surveillance or symptom-focused care fit your exact cancer and health. Supportive care can help during either pathway.

chapters.title: How pembrolizumab works
chapters.intro: This is an immunotherapy medicine.

items.title: Helping immune cells recognise cancer
items.text: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.

items.title: Why healthy organs can be affected
items.text: The immune system can also attack healthy tissues. Lung, bowel, liver, kidney, skin, gland, heart and nerve inflammation can range from mild to serious. Some hormone changes need long-term replacement.

items.title: A pause is a safety decision
items.text: Your team may delay a dose, treat side effects or stop pembrolizumab. The usual response to immune toxicity is to hold or stop treatment, not to give a smaller dose.

chapters.title: Your treatment course
chapters.intro: The appointment pattern and total duration are different decisions.

chapters.title: Tests and reviews
chapters.intro: Tell your team about symptoms even when recent blood tests were normal.

items.title: Before starting
items.text: Your team checks the cancer diagnosis, treatment aim and relevant tumour tests. Blood count, kidney/liver, glucose and thyroid tests provide a baseline. Discuss existing illnesses, medicines, pregnancy and breastfeeding.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose before every 3-week cycle; thyroid every 3–6 weeks, cortisol if indicated, and symptom review throughout and after treatment.

items.title: During a pause or after stopping
items.text: Extra tests may be needed for symptoms. Follow the agreed steroid or hormone plan. Keep your alert card and continue reporting symptoms after the last dose.

chapters.title: Practical support and everyday life
chapters.intro: Keep your team informed about what matters to you.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Fatigue can affect daily activities. Balance activity with rest and ask for help if tiredness is new, marked or accompanied by dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness; it may need medical assessment.

items.title: Eating, drinking and bowels
items.text: Drink as advised and report ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is a minor stomach upset; your team needs to check for immune inflammation and other causes.

items.title: Medicines and pregnancy
items.text: Bring a full medicine list, including supplements and steroids. Ask before starting new medicines. Use the contraception plan and discuss fertility or breastfeeding with your team.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Use the contact plan given by your oncology service.

items.title: Report warning symptoms
items.text: Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

items.title: During the drip
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately if you become itchy, flushed, breathless, dizzy, tight-chested or suddenly unwell.

items.title: Care after treatment ends
items.text: Immune inflammation can start late. Tell any healthcare team about pembrolizumab even after the course has finished.

rationale.summary: PD-1 blockade restores antitumour T-cell activity. First-line metastatic and post-resection adjuvant NSCLC have separate populations, treatment goals and evidence; the shared protocol does not make their eligibility interchangeable.
rationale.setting: Lung cancer only: first-line metastatic NSCLC or adjuvant NSCLC after surgery and platinum chemotherapy
rationale.line: First-line metastatic OR post-resection adjuvant after platinum chemotherapy
factors: Confirm the exact lung indication and treatment aim. Metastatic first-line: validated PD-L1 TPS ≥50%, no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation, stage IV, no prior systemic metastatic treatment, ECOG 0–1.

Adjuvant: complete resection, prior platinum chemotherapy, high recurrence-risk/pathological stage IB–IIIA AJCC7 source criteria, ECOG 0–1; confirm reimbursement/access separately. No metastatic TPS50 eligibility requirement applies.

FBC, renal and liver profiles, glucose and thyroid function. Review autoimmune disease, prior interstitial lung disease, infection, untreated brain metastases, steroid/immunosuppressive use, prior checkpoint treatment, pregnancy/breastfeeding and medicines.
alternatives: Choose among available systemic, targeted, clinical-trial, surveillance and supportive-care options using the precise setting, biomarkers, comorbidity and patient preferences.
limitations: These lung trials used pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks. Trial treatment limits and research scan schedules are not automatic NCCP prescribing rules.

KEYNOTE-024: selected untreated metastatic TPS≥50%, no sensitising EGFR/ALK; 66% effective crossover to subsequent PD-1/PD-L1 therapy in the chemotherapy group. Results are not for the adjuvant setting.

KEYNOTE-091 final DFS figures shown here are the adjuvant-chemotherapy subgroup (n=1,010), not all 1,177 randomized participants. At 46.7-month follow-up OS had only 58% of prespecified events; no established overall-survival advantage is claimed.
NCCP adjuvant NSCLC access is listed N/A; verify reimbursement. Trial schedules, efficacy and licensing are not identical to funded access.

before_each_cycle: Before each cycle: FBC, renal/liver profile and glucose; assess symptoms, immune toxicity and current medicines.
Check any new cough, breathlessness, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash, thirst/polyuria, fatigue, headache, weakness, chest pain or neurological change promptly; investigate alternative causes.
ongoing: Thyroid function every 3–6 weeks; on the 42-day schedule this is not every other cycle. Cortisol when clinically indicated, with sample timing and steroid context documented.
Disease imaging follows the supervising consultant plan. Clinically stable apparent early progression may need confirmation; do not automatically continue or stop without review.

Immune effects may persist or start after treatment ends. Maintain alert-card, urgent-contact and hormone-replacement follow-up; contraception during treatment and at least four months after the final dose.
administration: Pembrolizumab 200 mg is given as a drip over about 30 minutes on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). The hospital visit is longer because of checks and preparation.
Dilute in 100 mL sodium chloride 0.9%; final concentration 1–10 mg/mL. Use a sterile low-protein-binding 0.2–5 micrometre in-line/add-on filter. Verify source and pharmacy preparation policy.
access: Peripheral or other venous access per clinical assessment; anaphylaxis facilities available.
Monitor for infusion reactions; grade3–4 requires permanent discontinuation.

drug_mechanisms.pembrolizumab: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. evidence.trial: KEYNOTE-024 metastatic five-year follow-up; PEARLS/KEYNOTE-091 adjuvant study
evidence.population: KEYNOTE-024: 305 untreated metastatic NSCLC patients, TPS≥50%, no EGFR/ALK alterations. KEYNOTE-091: 1,177 resected stage IB (tumour ≥4 cm)–IIIA AJCC7 patients; final DFS figures below concern 1010 who received adjuvant chemotherapy.
evidence.comparison: KEYNOTE-024: pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (n=154, up to 35 cycles) versus platinum chemotherapy (n=151). KEYNOTE-091 chemotherapy subgroup: pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (n=506, approximately one year/18 doses) versus placebo (n=504).
evidence.applicability: These lung trials used pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks. Trial treatment limits and research scan schedules are not automatic NCCP prescribing rules.

endpoints.result_text: 31.9% versus 16.3%; median OS 26.3 versus 13.4 months; HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.48–0.81).
endpoints.interpretation: KEYNOTE-024; median follow-up 59.9 months, cutoff 1 June 2020. Population comparison, not an individual forecast.

endpoints.analysis_status: Final DFS; OS immature (58% of planned OS events overall)

support.title: Sickness medicines
support.text: Pembrolizumab alone has a minimal risk of causing sickness. Routine anti-sickness medicines or infusion premedicines are not usually needed; your team can prescribe symptom relief if required.

support.title: Immune alert card
support.text: Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

support.title: Hormones and steroids
support.text: Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines.

support.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least four months after the last dose. If pregnancy is possible or occurs, contact your oncology team promptly.

questions.q: Is my treatment for metastatic cancer or to reduce recurrence after surgery?
questions.a: Ask your team to write down the treatment aim. For metastatic disease, the aim is usually cancer control, symptom relief and more time. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence.

questions.q: Which tumour-test results support this plan?
questions.a: For the first-line metastatic monotherapy pathway, the source requires high PD-L1 expression and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. The adjuvant pathway has different eligibility. Ask which results apply to your own cancer.

questions.q: How long is my course, and what could change it?
questions.a: The adjuvant course lasts up to 12 months. Metastatic treatment continues while helpful and tolerable; a 24-month review may lead to stopping or continuing. Symptoms, response and your preferences can change the plan.

questions.q: Who arranges blood and thyroid tests between visits?
questions.a: The oncology team arranges and reviews tests. Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle; thyroid tests are usually every 3–6 weeks. Ask whether an extra test is needed between six-weekly infusions.

questions.q: Which symptoms should I report straight away, and whom do I contact out of hours?
questions.a: Report new or worsening breathing problems, persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, thirst or a spreading rash promptly. Keep the local oncology and out-of-hours numbers available; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs 112 / 999.

questions.q: What are my alternatives if I choose not to have this treatment?
questions.a: Ask about alternatives for your exact stage and tumour results, including other anticancer treatments, trials, surveillance where appropriate and symptom-focused care. Supportive care remains available whether or not you proceed.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be offered
evidence.intro: For suitable people with metastatic lung cancer and a high PD-L1 result, pembrolizumab helped people live longer than chemotherapy in a trial. After surgery and chemotherapy, a separate trial showed a lower risk of recurrence or death; longer-term overall survival was still uncertain at the reported analysis.
evidence.interpretation: These results describe groups of people, not what will happen to one person. The metastatic and after-surgery studies answer different questions.
evidence.population: Two separate lung settings: untreated metastatic PD-L1-high NSCLC; and resected NSCLC at high recurrence risk after chemotherapy.
evidence.limitations: The lung trials below used 200 mg every 3 weeks. The 400 mg every 6 weeks schedule is supported by drug-exposure modelling and regulatory bridging; it was not the randomized schedule in those lung trials.

chapters.title: Your lung cancer and treatment aim
chapters.intro: First confirm which lung setting applies to you.

items.title: Metastatic treatment
items.text: Metastatic means the cancer has spread. First-line means the first medicine treatment for this stage. Here, pembrolizumab alone is offered for suitable cancers with a high PD-L1 result and without EGFR or ALK alterations. The aim is usually control, symptom relief and more time.

items.title: After surgery
items.text: Adjuvant means treatment after surgery to reduce the chance of cancer returning. This pathway follows complete resection and platinum chemotherapy for cancer at high risk of recurrence. It does not use the same high PD-L1 requirement as the metastatic pathway.

items.title: Your alternatives
items.text: Ask which other treatments, clinical trials, surveillance or symptom-focused care fit your exact cancer and health. Supportive care can help during either pathway.

chapters.title: How pembrolizumab works
chapters.intro: This is an immunotherapy medicine.

items.title: Helping immune cells recognise cancer
items.text: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.

items.title: Why healthy organs can be affected
items.text: The immune system can also attack healthy tissues. Lung, bowel, liver, kidney, skin, gland, heart and nerve inflammation can range from mild to serious. Some hormone changes need long-term replacement.

items.title: A pause is a safety decision
items.text: Your team may delay a dose, treat side effects or stop pembrolizumab. The usual response to immune toxicity is to hold or stop treatment, not to give a smaller dose.

chapters.title: Your treatment course
chapters.intro: The appointment pattern and total duration are different decisions.

items.title: Changing schedules

chapters.title: Tests and reviews
chapters.intro: Tell your team about symptoms even when recent blood tests were normal.

items.title: Before starting
items.text: Your team checks the cancer diagnosis, treatment aim and relevant tumour tests. Blood count, kidney/liver, glucose and thyroid tests provide a baseline. Discuss existing illnesses, medicines, pregnancy and breastfeeding.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose before every 6-week cycle; thyroid every 3–6 weeks, cortisol if indicated, and symptom review throughout and after treatment.

items.title: During a pause or after stopping

chapters.title: Practical support and everyday life
chapters.intro: Keep your team informed about what matters to you.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Fatigue can affect daily activities. Balance activity with rest and ask for help if tiredness is new, marked or accompanied by dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness; it may need medical assessment.

items.title: Eating, drinking and bowels
items.text: Drink as advised and report ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is a minor stomach upset; your team needs to check for immune inflammation and other causes.

items.title: Medicines and pregnancy
items.text: Bring a full medicine list, including supplements and steroids. Ask before starting new medicines. Use the contraception plan and discuss fertility or breastfeeding with your team.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help

items.title: Report warning symptoms
items.text: Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

items.title: During the drip
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately if you become itchy, flushed, breathless, dizzy, tight-chested or suddenly unwell.

patient.title: Pembrolizumab + pemetrexed + cisplatin
patient.purpose: This combination aims to control metastatic non-squamous lung cancer, help symptoms and extend life. Your team weighs likely benefit, risks and what matters to you.

agents.name: Pembrolizumab
agents.explanation: PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops.
agents.watch: The immune system can also inflame healthy organs. New cough, diarrhoea, unusual weakness, severe headache, thirst or a spreading rash need prompt advice. Effects can start during treatment or after it finishes.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, glands, skin and other organs
Effects can develop after treatment ends

agents.name: Pemetrexed
agents.explanation: Pemetrexed is an antifolate: it blocks several enzymes that cells use to turn folate-dependent materials into DNA and RNA building blocks. With fewer building blocks, cancer cells have more difficulty copying their genetic instructions and dividing. Healthy rapidly renewing tissues, including bone marrow and the mouth lining, can also be affected. That helps explain low blood counts and mouth soreness. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce toxicity; they are part of the treatment, not supplements to omit because the drug is an antifolate.
agents.watch: Healthy tissues can be affected too: low blood counts, a sore mouth, rash and kidney problems are important. Folic acid, vitamin B12 and prescribed steroids help reduce particular risks.
risks: Fatigue, nausea, mouth soreness and rash
Kidney toxicity; folate and B12 supplementation are required

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that disrupt copying and repair, helping kill cancer cells. Healthy tissues can also be affected. Kidney, hearing and nerve effects are important; blood tests, symptom checks and prescribed hydration help the team manage risk.
agents.watch: Report reduced urine, ringing in the ears, hearing changes or tingling before the next treatment. Tell the nurse immediately about swelling or pain around the drip, rash, chest tightness or feeling suddenly unwell.

day_groups.action: Use the urgent advice below for fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell, including with a normal temperature.

day_groups.title: Prepare for your next review
day_groups.body: Some symptoms may settle; others can continue or appear for the first time. Improvement does not prove your blood counts have recovered. The next treatment depends on your review and tests.
day_groups.action: Bring your symptom record and questions. Confirm the next appointment: the next Day 1 is usually 21 days after this cycle's Day 1, if treatment proceeds.

support.title: Induction support
support.text: You receive anti-sickness medicines and a fluid plan around cisplatin. Take prescribed folic acid, B12 injections and rash-prevention steroids. Ask for one clear steroid schedule.

support.title: Maintenance support
support.text: Folic acid, B12 and rash-prevention medicines continue with pemetrexed; cisplatin fluids and some anti-sickness medicines may stop. Immune symptom vigilance continues.

questions.q: How will we know if it is helping?
questions.a: Ask your oncologist what the treatment is aiming to achieve for you, when scans are planned and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping it. How you feel and the amount of side effects do not reliably show how well treatment is working.

questions.q: Why might a cycle be delayed?
questions.a: A delay can give time to recover or investigate a new symptom. It is a safety decision, not a personal failure. Ask which medicines are affected, what needs to improve and when you will be reviewed.

questions.q: Will I get every side effect?
questions.a: No. The body map shows selected possibilities, not a prediction. Ask about common effects, serious less common effects, and any long-term risks that matter particularly to you. The same symptom can have several causes.

questions.q: What should I organise before starting?
questions.a: Confirm blood-test and Day Ward arrangements, transport home, your medicines schedule and a thermometer. Keep the oncology contact instructions and immunotherapy alert card available. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information if useful.

questions.q: What else belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: Your priorities, expected benefit, alternatives including supportive care, fertility, contraception, pregnancy or breastfeeding, work, driving and the possibility of lasting side effects. You can ask more questions or reconsider treatment at any stage.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean the treatment is working better?
questions.a: No. Side effects are not a reliable personal measure of cancer response. Report them so they can be treated; do not tolerate serious symptoms in the hope that they are a sign of benefit.

questions.q: Do all three medicines continue indefinitely?
questions.a: Induction: all three medicines on Day 1 every 21 days for up to four cycles. Maintenance: cisplatin stops; pembrolizumab and pemetrexed may continue every 21 days while appropriate. The team agrees duration and review points.

questions.q: What should I say when calling about a symptom?
questions.a: Give the current medicines or say you are in maintenance, the last treatment date, what changed and when, your temperature and whether you can eat, drink and pass urine. Do not delay calling to collect every detail.

questions.q: Which checks continue afterwards?
questions.a: Response imaging follows the consultant plan; no fixed universal scan interval is specified in these NCCP regimens. Immune toxicity can arise after the final pembrolizumab dose. Continue symptom vigilance, immunotherapy alert card and the team’s follow-up plan. Continue folic acid during pemetrexed and for 21 days after its last dose; B12 every three cycles while pemetrexed remains active.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis and treatment aim
chapters.intro: Start here if the names and abbreviations are new. You can read one section at a time and return when you need it.

items.title: What do the cancer terms mean?
items.text: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a broad group of lung cancers. “Non-squamous” describes the cells seen by the pathologist and includes adenocarcinoma. “Metastatic” means the cancer has spread beyond its original site. “First-line” means the first drug treatment chosen for this stage of illness. A regimen is a planned combination and schedule of medicines.

items.title: What is the treatment trying to achieve?
items.text: The usual aims in this setting are to control cancer, help symptoms and extend life while preserving quality of life. It is generally not given with an expectation of cure. Some people have prolonged benefit; others do not respond. Ask what success would look like for you: easier breathing, less pain, stable scans, more time or a balance of these.

items.title: Why are tumour tests important?
items.text: The team considers the cancer’s molecular results and PD-L1 result alongside your health. EGFR and ALK alterations can point towards a different treatment approach. PD-L1 is a protein involved in immune signalling; its result helps inform choices but is not a guarantee of benefit. This combination has evidence across PD-L1 groups, including low expression. Ask whether all relevant tumour testing is complete before your plan is finalised.

items.title: What are the alternatives?
items.text: The right comparison depends on tumour tests, symptoms, fitness and your preferences. Ask whether targeted therapy, immunotherapy alone, a different chemotherapy approach, a clinical trial or symptom-focused care is relevant. Supportive and palliative care can accompany active cancer treatment: help with breathlessness, pain, appetite and family concerns is not reserved for the last days of life.

chapters.title: Before the first infusion
chapters.intro: Use this as a conversation checklist. Your own hospital’s instructions and prescription take priority.

items.title: Tell the team your starting point
items.text: Describe your usual breathing, bowel pattern, energy, skin symptoms and ability to manage daily tasks. Mention autoimmune illness, organ transplant, previous lung inflammation, infections and all regular medicines. Changes are easier to recognise when the team knows what is normal for you. Do not minimise symptoms because you are worried treatment will be delayed.

items.title: Make the first week manageable
items.text: Have the oncology and out-of-hours numbers available, a working thermometer, your medicine schedule and a way to get urgent help. Ask who to ring if you miss a supportive medicine. Plan transport and practical help if needed. Bring your questions and, if you wish, someone you trust to listen and take notes.

items.title: During the infusion visit
items.text: Expect a symptom review and checks before drugs are released. Treatment is given through a cannula or another agreed venous access device. Tell the nurse immediately about burning or swelling around the drip, itching, flushing, dizziness or breathing changes. Waiting, pharmacy preparation and observation add to the time spent receiving the medicines.

chapters.title: What your tests and scans are checking
chapters.intro: Different checks answer different questions: whether treatment is safe today, whether a symptom needs investigation, and whether the cancer is responding.

items.title: Blood counts: three separate jobs
items.text: Neutrophils help fight infection; a low level can make infection dangerous. Haemoglobin carries oxygen; a low level can contribute to tiredness and breathlessness. Platelets help stop bleeding; low levels can cause bruising or bleeding. Feeling well does not prove your counts are normal, and a previous normal result does not rule out a new problem.

items.title: Kidney, liver and hormone checks
items.text: Kidney tests help assess whether cisplatin and pemetrexed are safe; cisplatin also needs a prescribed hydration plan. Liver tests can show injury before obvious symptoms develop. Pembrolizumab can disturb hormone-producing glands, so blood glucose and thyroid monitoring matter too. Symptoms can prompt additional tests. Always report how you feel: routine blood tests alone do not exclude every immune side effect.

items.title: Scans and the treatment decision
items.text: Your team sets the scan schedule and compares scans with symptoms and examination findings. Stable disease can be a worthwhile result. New symptoms need review even before the next scan. An unusual scan pattern sometimes needs clarification; do not assume that apparent growth is simply an immune response or that feeling worse means treatment is working.

items.title: Why a delay or a change can be appropriate
items.text: A pause may allow recovery or investigation. Chemotherapy doses can sometimes be reduced. Pembrolizumab is generally held or stopped for relevant toxicity rather than dose-reduced. Ask which drug is changing and why; stopping one drug does not automatically mean stopping every part of the plan. Long-term treatment decisions belong in a discussion about benefit, risk and what matters to you.

chapters.title: Side effects: what they mean and what to do
chapters.intro: These are selected possibilities, not a prediction or a complete medicine leaflet. You do not need to work out the cause before asking for help.

items.title: Nausea, vomiting and appetite change
items.text: Medicines can stimulate sickness pathways in the gut and brain. Take preventive anti-sickness medicines as prescribed, even when you initially feel well. Smaller meals and frequent sips may be easier. Report poor control early so the plan can be adjusted. Persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or much less urine need prompt advice. Do not wait until you are very dehydrated.

items.title: Fatigue: common, but not always “just treatment”
items.text: Fatigue may reflect treatment, disturbed sleep, reduced intake, anaemia or another illness. Balance rest with manageable movement and prioritise activities that matter to you. A sudden change, severe weakness, dizziness, breathlessness or inability to manage basic tasks needs assessment; hormone problems and other complications can resemble ordinary tiredness. Tell the team how fatigue affects daily life, not just that you feel tired.

items.title: Mouth soreness, ulcers and taste
items.text: Treatment can injure the lining of the mouth. Use a soft toothbrush, gentle mouth care and the rinses recommended by your team. Choose softer foods and avoid foods that sting. Ask for pain relief early. Report ulcers, white patches, painful swallowing or reduced intake; difficulty drinking or fever needs urgent advice. Arrange dental care with the oncology team before procedures.

items.title: Diarrhoea or abdominal pain
items.text: Pemetrexed can affect the bowel, but pembrolizumab can also cause bowel inflammation (colitis). Report new diarrhoea promptly, including how many stools above your normal pattern, blood or mucus, night-time symptoms and pain. Do not assume it is a harmless expected effect or rely on anti-diarrhoeal medicine without the team’s instructions. Severe pain, bleeding or dehydration needs urgent assessment.

items.title: Constipation
items.text: Anti-sickness drugs, opioid painkillers, less food and less movement can slow the bowel. Ask about a bowel plan if you are prone to constipation or take opioids. Keep track of your usual pattern. Increasing abdominal pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen or inability to pass wind needs prompt assessment rather than simply increasing laxatives.

items.title: Bruising, bleeding or breathlessness
items.text: Chemotherapy may reduce platelets or red cells. Report unexpected bruises, nosebleeds, bleeding gums or increasing breathlessness. Heavy bleeding, black stools with weakness, severe chest pain or severe breathing difficulty need emergency help. Do not start iron or alter blood thinners without review: the cause and treatment need to be established.

items.title: Skin, hair, nerves and hearing
items.text: Skin can become dry, itchy or develop a rash; report new changes, especially if spreading. Hair may thin. Tingling, numbness or hearing changes should be reported before the next dose because they may affect the plan. Blisters, peeling skin or sores involving the eyes or mouth need urgent assessment. Use gentle skin care and discuss suitable sun protection.

chapters.title: Pembrolizumab: symptoms that deserve special attention
chapters.intro: Immune treatment can cause inflammation in healthy organs, during treatment or after it ends. Keep your immunotherapy alert card and tell other healthcare professionals you have received pembrolizumab.

items.title: Lungs, bowel, liver and kidneys
items.text: New cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced urine or swelling can signal inflammation. These symptoms also have other causes, including infection and cancer. Contact the team promptly for assessment rather than trying to identify the organ or diagnosis yourself.

items.title: Hormones, heart and nervous system
items.text: Report unusual weakness, persistent headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, palpitations, muscle weakness or changes in vision. Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion, seizures or major breathing difficulty require emergency care. Some hormone effects need ongoing replacement treatment even after immunotherapy stops.

items.title: Why early reporting matters
items.text: The team may pause treatment and investigate. Some reactions need steroids or other immune-suppressing treatment; others need hormone replacement. These are different from the short planned steroid course around chemotherapy. Do not start leftover steroids, change their dose or stop a prescribed course yourself. Carry the treatment name when attending emergency care.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: The aim is a plan that fits your life as well as your treatment. Bring practical concerns to the team early.

items.title: Food, fluids and weight
items.text: Aim for enough food and fluid to maintain strength, using foods you tolerate. Tell the team about weight loss, swallowing problems or difficulty shopping or cooking; ask for dietitian support. A fixed fluid target is not right for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney disease. “Anti-cancer” diets, fasting and high-dose supplements are not substitutes for treatment and can create nutritional or interaction problems.

items.title: Movement, work and rest
items.text: Try activity that feels manageable and increase or reduce it according to symptoms. Short walks or simple daily tasks may be more realistic than your usual exercise. Discuss work adjustments and travel plans. Do not drive if dizzy, unusually tired or affected by sedating medicines. Sudden deterioration should prompt assessment, not an attempt to push through exercise.

items.title: Infection precautions without isolation
items.text: Wash hands, practise food hygiene and avoid close contact with people who are unwell. Ask about vaccinations and their timing; some vaccines are unsuitable during treatment. You can usually still spend time with family. Keep your urgent contact plan available: precautions reduce risk but do not make fever or sudden illness safe to watch at home.

items.title: Intimacy, fertility and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment if relevant. Treatment may harm a developing baby; ask for a written contraception plan covering all three medicines and the period after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment; confirm when it would be safe to restart. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Ask about barrier protection and handling body fluids under your hospital’s advice.

items.title: Emotional support and choices
items.text: It is reasonable to feel worried, angry, uncertain or overloaded. Ask for psycho-oncology, counselling, social work or family support. You can request information in smaller pieces, an interpreter or a written summary. Tell the team what you most want to preserve in daily life. You can revisit treatment decisions and ask for more time or another explanation.

chapters.title: A short treatment dictionary
chapters.intro: Terms you may hear in clinic.

items.title: Cycle · induction · maintenance
items.text: A cycle is a planned treatment-and-interval period. Induction is the initial combination phase. Maintenance is ongoing treatment after that phase; it does not mean side-effect-free treatment.

items.title: Response · stable disease · progression
items.text: Response means the cancer has reduced by the assessment used. Stable disease means it has not changed enough to meet response or progression criteria. Progression means growth or spread meeting the assessment criteria. Your team interprets these alongside how you are feeling.

items.title: Neutropenia · anaemia · thrombocytopenia
items.text: Neutropenia means low infection-fighting neutrophils. Anaemia means low haemoglobin. Thrombocytopenia means low platelets. These are different results with different implications; one normal number does not establish that all treatment risks are low.

items.title: Immune-related · colitis · pneumonitis
items.text: Immune-related effects come from immune activity against healthy tissue. Colitis means inflammation of the colon; pneumonitis means inflammation in the lungs. A symptom alone cannot establish either diagnosis.

chapters.title: Cisplatin: hydration, hearing and nerves
chapters.intro: These checks belong to the cisplatin phase. Problems that continue after it stops still need review.

items.title: Fluids and electrolytes
items.text: You receive prescribed fluids around cisplatin. The amount and timing depend on your health and local policy; do not force a fixed fluid target if you have heart or kidney disease. Report reduced urine, swelling, dizziness or persistent vomiting.

items.title: Hearing and nerve changes
items.text: Tell the team about ringing in the ears, changed hearing, numbness or difficulty with fine movements before the next dose. Some effects can last; early reporting helps guide treatment decisions.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: Adding pembrolizumab to chemotherapy improved survival and delayed progression in the trial population. Results cannot predict one person’s benefit.
evidence.interpretation: Adding pembrolizumab to chemotherapy improved survival and delayed progression in the trial population. Results cannot predict one person’s benefit.
evidence.population: People with previously untreated metastatic non-squamous lung cancer without EGFR/ALK alterations.
evidence.limitations: The randomised comparison pooled cisplatin and carboplatin; these figures are not a cisplatin-specific treatment effect.

patient.title: Pembrolizumab + paclitaxel + carboplatin AUC6
patient.purpose: This combination aims to control metastatic squamous lung cancer, help symptoms and extend life. Your team weighs likely benefit, risks and what matters to you.

agents.name: Pembrolizumab
agents.explanation: PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops.
agents.watch: The immune system can also inflame healthy organs. New cough, diarrhoea, unusual weakness, severe headache, thirst or a spreading rash need prompt advice. Effects can start during treatment or after it finishes.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, glands, skin and other organs
Effects can develop after treatment ends

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Paclitaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules that cells need to divide. This disrupts cancer-cell division. Healthy tissues can be affected too, including blood-forming cells and nerves. That explains why infection risk, hair loss and numbness or tingling matter during treatment.
agents.watch: Report numbness, tingling or difficulty using your hands before the next dose. During the infusion, tell the nurse immediately about itching, flushing, chest tightness, back pain or feeling faint.
risks: Numbness or tingling that may persist

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapy. Inside cells, it forms chemical attachments to DNA, including links that stop DNA strands working normally. This disrupts copying and repair and can lead to cell death. Healthy cells can also be injured, especially blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. The kidneys help remove carboplatin, so kidney function is used to calculate the dose. AUC 6 describes a target drug exposure over time; it is not a fixed dose of 6 mg.
agents.watch: Low blood counts, nausea and vomiting can occur. An allergic reaction is also possible: tell the nurse immediately if you feel flushed, itchy, tight-chested or unwell during the drip.
risks: Low blood counts, infection or bleeding

day_groups.title: Your infusion day
day_groups.body: Your team checks symptoms and blood results before treatment. Tell your nurse immediately about pain at the drip site, itching, flushing or breathing changes. The time in hospital includes checks and preparation, not just infusion time.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, check your take-home medicines, contact details and next appointment.

day_groups.title: The first days at home
day_groups.body: Feeling sick can start on treatment day or later. Appetite, taste, sleep or bowel habits may change. Take prescribed supportive medicines as directed; ask for help if they are not controlling symptoms.
day_groups.action: Contact the team if vomiting persists, you cannot keep fluids down, or you develop new diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is ordinary chemotherapy upset.

day_groups.title: Keep checking how you feel
day_groups.body: Blood counts may be reduced between treatments. You cannot tell your count from the date or from how well you feel. Fatigue or mouth symptoms may affect eating and daily activity.
day_groups.action: Use the urgent advice below for fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell, including with a normal temperature.

day_groups.title: Prepare for your next review
day_groups.body: Some symptoms may settle; others can continue or appear for the first time. Improvement does not prove your blood counts have recovered. The next treatment depends on your review and tests.
day_groups.action: Bring your symptom record and questions. Confirm the next appointment: the next Day 1 is usually 21 days after this cycle's Day 1, if treatment proceeds.

support.title: Induction support
support.text: Anti-sickness medicines help with carboplatin. Paclitaxel premedication helps prevent infusion reactions. Ask for one clear steroid schedule and report infusion symptoms immediately.

support.title: Maintenance support
support.text: Chemotherapy and taxane premedication stop. Pembrolizumab alone usually does not need the same preventive anti-sickness medicines; ask for the updated prescription. Immune symptom vigilance continues.

questions.q: How will we know if it is helping?
questions.a: Ask your oncologist what the treatment is aiming to achieve for you, when scans are planned and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping it. How you feel and the amount of side effects do not reliably show how well treatment is working.

questions.q: Why might a cycle be delayed?
questions.a: A delay can give time to recover or investigate a new symptom. It is a safety decision, not a personal failure. Ask which medicines are affected, what needs to improve and when you will be reviewed.

questions.q: Will I get every side effect?
questions.a: No. The body map shows selected possibilities, not a prediction. Ask about common effects, serious less common effects, and any long-term risks that matter particularly to you. The same symptom can have several causes.

questions.q: What should I organise before starting?
questions.a: Confirm blood-test and Day Ward arrangements, transport home, your medicines schedule and a thermometer. Keep the oncology contact instructions and immunotherapy alert card available. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information if useful.

questions.q: What else belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: Your priorities, expected benefit, alternatives including supportive care, fertility, contraception, pregnancy or breastfeeding, work, driving and the possibility of lasting side effects. You can ask more questions or reconsider treatment at any stage.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean the treatment is working better?
questions.a: No. Side effects are not a reliable personal measure of cancer response. Report them so they can be treated; do not tolerate serious symptoms in the hope that they are a sign of benefit.

questions.q: Do all three medicines continue indefinitely?
questions.a: Induction: all three medicines on Day 1 every 21 days for up to four cycles. Maintenance: paclitaxel and carboplatin stop; pembrolizumab alone may continue every 21 days while appropriate. The team agrees duration and review points.

questions.q: What should I say when calling about a symptom?
questions.a: Give the current medicines or say you are in maintenance, the last treatment date, what changed and when, your temperature and whether you can eat, drink and pass urine. Do not delay calling to collect every detail.

questions.q: Which checks continue afterwards?
questions.a: Response imaging follows the consultant plan; no fixed universal scan interval is specified in these NCCP regimens. Immune toxicity can arise after the final pembrolizumab dose. Continue symptom vigilance, immunotherapy alert card and the team’s follow-up plan. Review persistent neuropathy, hearing effects and cytopenias even after chemotherapy stops; immunotherapy maintenance has a different supportive-care plan.

chapters.title: Understanding the treatment aim
chapters.intro: Take one section at a time and discuss what matters to you.

items.title: What do the words mean?
items.text: Squamous describes the lung-cancer cells seen by the pathologist. Metastatic means the cancer has spread beyond its original site. First-line means the first drug treatment for this stage. This regimen combines chemotherapy with an immune treatment.

items.title: What is treatment trying to achieve?
items.text: The usual aims are cancer control, symptom relief and longer life while considering quality of life. It is generally not given with an expectation of cure. Some people have a prolonged response; others do not. Your team uses your cancer tests, general health and preferences to choose a plan.

items.title: What are the alternatives?
items.text: Ask whether another chemotherapy/immunotherapy option, a clinical trial or symptom-focused care is appropriate. Supportive and palliative care can accompany active treatment. PD-L1 helps inform choices, but this combination’s trial included people across PD-L1 groups and a result does not guarantee benefit.

chapters.title: Before the first infusion
chapters.intro: Your hospital’s instructions take priority.

items.title: Tell the team your starting point
items.text: Describe usual breathing, bowel pattern, energy, skin and nerve symptoms. Mention autoimmune illness, previous lung inflammation, infection and all medicines including steroids and supplements. Changes are easier to recognise when the team knows what is normal for you.

items.title: Prepare the practical details
items.text: Keep the oncology and out-of-hours numbers, a thermometer and the immunotherapy alert card available. Check blood-test appointments, transport and who can help at home. Ask for written medicine directions and accessible information.

items.title: What happens on the day?
items.text: Blood results and symptoms are reviewed before release of treatment. Pembrolizumab is followed by paclitaxel and then carboplatin during induction. Premedication helps reduce paclitaxel reactions. Tell the nurse immediately about drip-site pain, itching, flushing, chest/back pain, dizziness or breathing changes.

chapters.title: What tests and scans check
chapters.intro: A normal earlier test does not rule out a new problem.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils help fight infection, platelets help stop bleeding, and red cells carry oxygen. Counts can fall between visits. You cannot know a count from the day of the cycle or from feeling well.

items.title: Kidneys, liver and hormones
items.text: Kidney function helps determine the carboplatin dose. Liver tests influence paclitaxel safety. Pembrolizumab can affect hormone-producing glands, so glucose and thyroid monitoring continue in maintenance. Report symptoms even if routine tests are normal.

items.title: Scans and treatment review
items.text: The team sets the scan schedule and reviews scans with symptoms and examination. Stable cancer can be a worthwhile result. Report new symptoms before the next scan; do not assume worsening is evidence that immune treatment is working.

items.title: Delays and changed doses
items.text: Chemotherapy may be delayed or reduced for toxicity. Pembrolizumab is held or stopped for relevant toxicity rather than dose-reduced. Ask which medicine is changing and why. Omitted checks are not the same as normal results.

chapters.title: Side effects and what to do
chapters.intro: Selected possibilities are shown; this is not a prediction or a complete medicine leaflet.

items.title: Nausea, vomiting and appetite
items.text: Take prescribed anti-sickness medicines as directed. Small meals and regular sips may help. Report poor control early; persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or much less urine needs prompt advice.

items.title: Fatigue and weakness
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Sudden severe weakness, dizziness, breathlessness or inability to manage basic tasks needs assessment: infection, anaemia or hormone problems can resemble ordinary tiredness.

items.title: Mouth and bowels
items.text: Use gentle mouth care and report painful ulcers or difficulty drinking. Report new diarrhoea, abdominal pain or blood in stools promptly because immune bowel inflammation is possible. Ask about constipation from anti-sickness drugs or pain medicines; severe pain, swelling or vomiting needs assessment.

items.title: Hair, skin, muscles and nerves
items.text: Paclitaxel commonly causes hair loss and may cause muscle/joint aches and numbness or tingling. Report nerve symptoms before the next dose, especially if balance or hand function changes. Blisters, peeling skin or sores around eyes/mouth need urgent advice.

items.title: Bruising and bleeding
items.text: Report unusual bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding gums. Heavy bleeding, black stools with weakness or severe breathlessness needs urgent assessment. Do not change prescribed blood thinners without advice.

chapters.title: Pembrolizumab: symptoms that deserve special attention
chapters.intro: Immune treatment can cause inflammation in healthy organs, during treatment or after it ends. Keep your immunotherapy alert card and tell other healthcare professionals you have received pembrolizumab.

items.title: Lungs, bowel, liver and kidneys
items.text: New cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced urine or swelling can signal inflammation. These symptoms also have other causes, including infection and cancer. Contact the team promptly for assessment rather than trying to identify the organ or diagnosis yourself.

items.title: Hormones, heart and nervous system
items.text: Report unusual weakness, persistent headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, palpitations, muscle weakness or changes in vision. Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion, seizures or major breathing difficulty require emergency care. Some hormone effects need ongoing replacement treatment even after immunotherapy stops.

items.title: Why early reporting matters
items.text: The team may pause treatment and investigate. Some reactions need steroids or other immune-suppressing treatment; others need hormone replacement. These are different from the short planned steroid course around chemotherapy. Do not start leftover steroids, change their dose or stop a prescribed course yourself. Carry the treatment name when attending emergency care.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: The aim is a plan that fits your life as well as your treatment. Bring practical concerns to the team early.

items.title: Food, fluids and weight
items.text: Aim for enough food and fluid to maintain strength, using foods you tolerate. Tell the team about weight loss, swallowing problems or difficulty shopping or cooking; ask for dietitian support. A fixed fluid target is not right for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney disease. “Anti-cancer” diets, fasting and high-dose supplements are not substitutes for treatment and can create nutritional or interaction problems.

items.title: Movement, work and rest
items.text: Try activity that feels manageable and increase or reduce it according to symptoms. Short walks or simple daily tasks may be more realistic than your usual exercise. Discuss work adjustments and travel plans. Do not drive if dizzy, unusually tired or affected by sedating medicines. Sudden deterioration should prompt assessment, not an attempt to push through exercise.

items.title: Infection precautions without isolation
items.text: Wash hands, practise food hygiene and avoid close contact with people who are unwell. Ask about vaccinations and their timing; some vaccines are unsuitable during treatment. You can usually still spend time with family. Keep your urgent contact plan available: precautions reduce risk but do not make fever or sudden illness safe to watch at home.

items.title: Intimacy, fertility and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment if relevant. Treatment may harm a developing baby; ask for a written contraception plan covering all three medicines and the period after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment; confirm when it would be safe to restart. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Ask about barrier protection and handling body fluids under your hospital’s advice.

items.title: Emotional support and choices
items.text: It is reasonable to feel worried, angry, uncertain or overloaded. Ask for psycho-oncology, counselling, social work or family support. You can request information in smaller pieces, an interpreter or a written summary. Tell the team what you most want to preserve in daily life. You can revisit treatment decisions and ask for more time or another explanation.

chapters.title: A short treatment dictionary
chapters.intro: Terms you may hear in clinic.

items.title: Cycle · induction · maintenance
items.text: A cycle is a planned treatment-and-interval period. Induction is the initial combination phase. Maintenance is ongoing treatment after that phase; it does not mean side-effect-free treatment.

items.title: Response · stable disease · progression
items.text: Response means the cancer has reduced by the assessment used. Stable disease means it has not changed enough to meet response or progression criteria. Progression means growth or spread meeting the assessment criteria. Your team interprets these alongside how you are feeling.

items.title: Neutropenia · anaemia · thrombocytopenia
items.text: Neutropenia means low infection-fighting neutrophils. Anaemia means low haemoglobin. Thrombocytopenia means low platelets. These are different results with different implications; one normal number does not establish that all treatment risks are low.

items.title: Immune-related · colitis · pneumonitis
items.text: Immune-related effects come from immune activity against healthy tissue. Colitis means inflammation of the colon; pneumonitis means inflammation in the lungs. A symptom alone cannot establish either diagnosis.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: Adding pembrolizumab to chemotherapy improved survival and delayed progression in the trial population. Results cannot predict one person’s benefit.
evidence.interpretation: Adding pembrolizumab to chemotherapy improved survival and delayed progression in the trial population. Results cannot predict one person’s benefit.
evidence.population: People with previously untreated metastatic squamous lung cancer.
evidence.limitations: The randomised comparison pooled paclitaxel and nab-paclitaxel; these figures are not an isolated estimate for paclitaxel 200 mg/m².

agents.name: Durvalumab
agents.explanation: Durvalumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can reduce the immune system’s ability to attack cancer cells. Removing this signal can help immune cells act against cancer, but the immune system can also inflame healthy organs.
agents.mechanism: Blocks PD-L1 to support immune recognition of cancer
visual: PD-L1 can dampen an immune response
Immune cells can act against cancer cells
risks: Inflammation of the lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys or skin
Thyroid, adrenal, pituitary or blood-sugar problems that may need long-term replacement treatment
Rare serious inflammation of the heart, muscles or nerves
Infusion reactions, fatigue and infections; effects can appear after treatment ends
agents.watch: Report new symptoms early and carry the immunotherapy alert card. Do not wait for the next infusion.

anatomy: Report new or worsening cough, breathlessness or chest pain promptly, including after finishing radiotherapy.
Severe headache, dizziness, confusion, unusual weakness or thirst need prompt assessment; collapse or seizures need emergency help.
Chest pain, palpitations, marked weakness or trouble swallowing can signal serious inflammation; seek urgent help.
Report yellow eyes/skin, dark urine or significant upper abdominal pain; blood tests may detect changes before symptoms.
Report new diarrhoea, blood in stools or significant abdominal pain; do not assume this is ordinary stomach upset.
Report much less urine, swelling or a change in urine; attend kidney blood tests.
Report a spreading rash. Blistering, peeling or mouth/eye sores need urgent assessment.
patient.anatomy_note: These are examples of immune side effects, not a diagnosis or a complete list. Symptoms may have other causes, and blood tests can detect inflammation before you feel it.

sections.title: Two different parts of treatment
sections.text: Platinum chemotherapy and radiation are given together first. Durvalumab follows after that course has finished and the team has confirmed that the cancer has not progressed.

sections.title: Infusion visits
sections.text: The usual reference dose is 10 mg/kg, given into a vein over about 60 minutes every 14 days. Allow extra time for the clinical review, tests and preparation.

sections.title: Bloods, scans and transport
sections.text: Confirm where blood tests are taken, who reviews them and the planned clinic/scan appointments. Allow extra time at the treatment unit and arrange help with travel if fatigue or symptoms make it difficult.

sections.title: A pause or early finish
sections.text: Treatment can be paused to investigate symptoms or treat an immune reaction. A missed dose does not automatically extend the course beyond the planned maximum. Restart decisions belong to the consultant team.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Durvalumab is given after definitive chemoradiotherapy to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning or worsening and improve the chance of longer survival. This is part of a treatment pathway that aims for long-term control and possible cure; it cannot guarantee cure.
evidence.population: Unresectable stage III NSCLC after concurrent platinum chemoradiotherapy, without progression
evidence.interpretation: In PACIFIC, durvalumab reduced cancer worsening and improved overall survival compared with placebo after chemoradiotherapy. The results describe groups of trial participants and do not predict what will happen to one person.
evidence.limitations: PACIFIC directly studied durvalumab every two weeks after concurrent chemoradiotherapy. This guide uses that interval. The study included people across PD-L1 groups; this NCCP regimen has its own PD-L1 eligibility requirement. Discuss expected benefit, side effects and alternatives for your situation.

patient.teachback: What is the sequence of chemoradiotherapy and durvalumab, how often are your infusions, what is the planned maximum course, and which symptoms mean you should contact the team immediately? Who should see your immunotherapy alert card?
patient.consent_support: Discuss the consolidation aim and possible benefit after chemoradiotherapy, alternatives and the option to decline; lung inflammation after chest radiation; immune inflammation of other organs; possible long-term hormone replacement; infusion reactions; reproductive precautions; tests, visits, the course cap and possible holds or permanent stopping. Trial results do not guarantee cure or individual benefit.

support.title: Immune side effects and the alert card
support.text: Immune side effects may start during treatment or after the last dose. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and tell every treating clinician that you have received durvalumab, even during a treatment break or after finishing.

support.title: Lung symptoms after radiotherapy
support.text: Radiation inflammation, immune inflammation, infection and cancer can cause similar symptoms. Report new or worsening breathing symptoms promptly so the team can assess the cause. Do not assume a new cough is only an old radiotherapy effect.

support.title: Support medicines
support.text: Durvalumab alone has minimal sickness risk and no routine premedication is specified. Use anti-sickness or other medicines only as prescribed. Steroids for an immune reaction are a treatment plan supervised by the team, not routine premedication; do not start, reduce or stop them yourself.

support.title: Hormone replacement and blood tests
support.text: Thyroid, adrenal or diabetes problems may need hormone replacement or insulin, sometimes long term. Keep taking prescribed medicines and attend blood tests even when you feel well. Sudden severe weakness, vomiting, faintness, unusual thirst or drowsiness need urgent advice.

support.title: Pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss pregnancy plans, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Effective contraception is advised during durvalumab and for at least three months after the last dose. Durvalumab is not recommended during pregnancy. The team must help decide whether breastfeeding or durvalumab should be stopped or avoided, weighing the benefits and risks.

questions.q: Is this more chemotherapy?
questions.a: Durvalumab is an immunotherapy infusion. It follows the completed chemotherapy and radiation course and works by changing immune signalling.

questions.q: How long will I receive it?
questions.a: Durvalumab is infused on Day 1 of each 14-day cycle. The course lasts up to 12 months (26 cycles), and can finish earlier if the cancer progresses or side effects make continuation unsuitable. The first dose should start within 42 days after chemoradiotherapy finishes.

questions.q: Why report a cough after chest radiotherapy?
questions.a: Radiation effects, immune inflammation, infection and cancer can look alike. The team needs to assess new or worsening symptoms rather than assume their cause.

questions.q: Will I need routine steroids before each infusion?
questions.a: No routine premedication is specified for this regimen. Steroids may be prescribed to treat particular immune side effects, with a supervised dose and taper.

questions.q: Can side effects happen after I stop?
questions.a: Immune side effects may start during treatment or after the last dose. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and tell every treating clinician that you have received durvalumab, even during a treatment break or after finishing.

rationale.summary: Durvalumab is given after definitive chemoradiotherapy to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning or worsening and improve the chance of longer survival. This is part of a treatment pathway that aims for long-term control and possible cure; it cannot guarantee cure.
rationale.setting: Consolidation for unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with no cancer progression and tumour PD-L1 of at least 1%.
rationale.line: Consolidation after definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy in a curative-intent stage III pathway; not metastatic first-line monotherapy.
factors: Confirm NCCP eligibility, PD-L1 testing, performance status, CRT details and recovery.
Balance durable control and survival evidence against post-radiation lung risk, immune adverse events, pre-existing disease and patient preferences.
Agree route, interval, maximum duration, test ownership, emergency contact and access/reimbursement.
alternatives: Individual alternatives, observation or another treatment pathway require multidisciplinary review of stage, biomarkers, CRT recovery, comorbidity and patient preferences; no cross-trial ranking is implied.
limitations: These NCCP codes cover post-concurrent-CRT consolidation for unresectable stage III NSCLC. They do not cover sequential CRT, resectable perioperative NSCLC, metastatic combination treatment or small-cell lung cancer, even though EMA lists other durvalumab indications.

Current NCCP eligibility requires PD-L1 ≥1%, ECOG 0–1, at least two concurrent platinum cycles, radiation ≥60 Gy, and no progression. PACIFIC enrolled irrespective of PD-L1; overall-trial results are not a PD-L1 ≥1% subgroup estimate.

PD-L1 subgroup analyses were exploratory/post hoc for the 1% threshold, with tissue unavailable for some patients and small subgroups. They cannot establish benefit or no benefit for an individual or replace NCCP eligibility.
PACIFIC directly studied durvalumab every two weeks after concurrent chemoradiotherapy. This guide uses that interval.

The numerical OS/PFS results below come from the same exploratory five-year update with data cutoff 11 January 2021. They are not mixed with the original co-primary endpoint analyses or presented as individual benefit.
NCCP Table 1 explicitly uses CTCAE 4.03. Confirm the event-specific grade and alternative causes; general interface CTCAE5 aids are not a substitute for this source standard.

Current source hepatitis rows hold AST/ALT >3 through ≤10×ULN; the merged table cell includes >5–10. Stop above 10×ULN, bilirubin >3×ULN, or concurrent AST/ALT >3 and bilirubin >2 without an alternative cause. Do not copy another checkpoint inhibitor’s threshold.

General restart criteria require recovery to grade ≤1, steroid dose ≤10 mg/day prednisone equivalent and resumption within 12 weeks. Organ-specific permanent-stop rules take precedence. Controlled hormone-replacement endocrinopathies have a stated exception to the general severe/recurrent immune-event stop rule.
No durvalumab dose-reduction ladder is recommended for toxicity. Mild/moderate baseline renal or hepatic impairment requires no dose adjustment; data in severe impairment are limited.

clinical.component_rationale: Durvalumab binds PD-L1 and blocks its interaction with PD-1/CD80, supporting antitumour immune activity. It is given after the completed definitive concurrent CRT phase; its toxicity rules do not assess the earlier cytotoxic or radiation treatment.
key_points: Consolidation for unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with no cancer progression and tumour PD-L1 of at least 1%.

Durvalumab is infused on Day 1 of each 14-day cycle. The course lasts up to 12 months (26 cycles), and can finish earlier if the cancer progresses or side effects make continuation unsuitable. The first dose should start within 42 days after chemoradiotherapy finishes.
The usual reference dose is 10 mg/kg, given into a vein over about 60 minutes every 14 days. Allow extra time for the clinical review, tests and preparation.
Dose escalation/reduction is not recommended for toxicity; use hold/discontinue rules and specialist management.
New pulmonary symptoms after CRT require distinction among radiation pneumonitis, immune pneumonitis, infection and progression.
Source Table 1 is CTCAE4.03; stable treated hypothyroidism/type1 diabetes does not share the blanket hold rule for unstable hyperthyroid/adrenal/pituitary disease.

disease_and_biomarker_context: Consolidation for unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with no cancer progression and tumour PD-L1 of at least 1%.
eligibility_orientation: Confirm adult stage III unresectable NSCLC, validated PD-L1 ≥1%, no progression after ≥2 cycles of concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiation ≥60 Gy; ECOG 0–1.
Confirm the CRT completion-to-first-dose interval (≤42 days), plan maximum 12 months and the correct q14/q28 schedule.
important_cautions: Review CRT pneumonitis, autoimmune/IBD history, immunodeficiency, transplant, previous immunotherapy/irAEs, infection, systemic immunosuppression and reproductive considerations.

support_summary: Immune side effects may start during treatment or after the last dose. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and tell every treating clinician that you have received durvalumab, even during a treatment break or after finishing.

Radiation inflammation, immune inflammation, infection and cancer can cause similar symptoms. Report new or worsening breathing symptoms promptly so the team can assess the cause. Do not assume a new cough is only an old radiotherapy effect.

Durvalumab alone has minimal sickness risk and no routine premedication is specified. Use anti-sickness or other medicines only as prescribed. Steroids for an immune reaction are a treatment plan supervised by the team, not routine premedication; do not start, reduce or stop them yourself.

Thyroid, adrenal or diabetes problems may need hormone replacement or insulin, sometimes long term. Keep taking prescribed medicines and attend blood tests even when you feel well. Sudden severe weakness, vomiting, faintness, unusual thirst or drowsiness need urgent advice.

Discuss pregnancy plans, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Effective contraception is advised during durvalumab and for at least three months after the last dose. Durvalumab is not recommended during pregnancy. The team must help decide whether breastfeeding or durvalumab should be stopped or avoided, weighing the benefits and risks.
baseline: Confirm adult stage III unresectable NSCLC, validated PD-L1 ≥1%, no progression after ≥2 cycles of concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiation ≥60 Gy; ECOG 0–1.
Confirm the CRT completion-to-first-dose interval (≤42 days), plan maximum 12 months and the correct q14/q28 schedule.

before_each_cycle: Review current symptoms, new medicines/steroids, previous immune events, treatment holds and source course duration.
