limitations: These NCCP codes cover post-concurrent-CRT consolidation for unresectable stage III NSCLC. They do not cover sequential CRT, resectable perioperative NSCLC, metastatic combination treatment or small-cell lung cancer, even though EMA lists other durvalumab indications.

Current NCCP eligibility requires PD-L1 ≥1%, ECOG 0–1, at least two concurrent platinum cycles, radiation ≥60 Gy, and no progression. PACIFIC enrolled irrespective of PD-L1; overall-trial results are not a PD-L1 ≥1% subgroup estimate.

PD-L1 subgroup analyses were exploratory/post hoc for the 1% threshold, with tissue unavailable for some patients and small subgroups. They cannot establish benefit or no benefit for an individual or replace NCCP eligibility.
PACIFIC directly studied durvalumab every two weeks after concurrent chemoradiotherapy. This guide uses that interval.

Current source hepatitis rows hold AST/ALT >3 through ≤10×ULN; the merged table cell includes >5–10. Stop above 10×ULN, bilirubin >3×ULN, or concurrent AST/ALT >3 and bilirubin >2 without an alternative cause. Do not copy another checkpoint inhibitor’s threshold.

agents.name: Durvalumab
agents.explanation: Durvalumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can reduce the immune system’s ability to attack cancer cells. Removing this signal can help immune cells act against cancer, but the immune system can also inflame healthy organs.
agents.mechanism: Blocks PD-L1 to support immune recognition of cancer
visual: PD-L1 can dampen an immune response
Immune cells can act against cancer cells
risks: Inflammation of the lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys or skin
Thyroid, adrenal, pituitary or blood-sugar problems that may need long-term replacement treatment
Rare serious inflammation of the heart, muscles or nerves
Infusion reactions, fatigue and infections; effects can appear after treatment ends
agents.watch: Report new symptoms early and carry the immunotherapy alert card. Do not wait for the next infusion.

anatomy: Report new or worsening cough, breathlessness or chest pain promptly, including after finishing radiotherapy.
Severe headache, dizziness, confusion, unusual weakness or thirst need prompt assessment; collapse or seizures need emergency help.
Chest pain, palpitations, marked weakness or trouble swallowing can signal serious inflammation; seek urgent help.
Report yellow eyes/skin, dark urine or significant upper abdominal pain; blood tests may detect changes before symptoms.
Report new diarrhoea, blood in stools or significant abdominal pain; do not assume this is ordinary stomach upset.
Report much less urine, swelling or a change in urine; attend kidney blood tests.
Report a spreading rash. Blistering, peeling or mouth/eye sores need urgent assessment.
patient.anatomy_note: These are examples of immune side effects, not a diagnosis or a complete list. Symptoms may have other causes, and blood tests can detect inflammation before you feel it.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Durvalumab is given after definitive chemoradiotherapy to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning or worsening and improve the chance of longer survival. This is part of a treatment pathway that aims for long-term control and possible cure; it cannot guarantee cure.
evidence.population: Unresectable stage III NSCLC after concurrent platinum chemoradiotherapy, without progression
evidence.interpretation: In PACIFIC, durvalumab reduced cancer worsening and improved overall survival compared with placebo after chemoradiotherapy. The results describe groups of trial participants and do not predict what will happen to one person.
evidence.limitations: PACIFIC studied durvalumab every two weeks. The every-four-week schedule is supported by regulatory drug-exposure bridging; PACIFIC did not directly compare these two schedules or test this fixed dose as its randomised treatment. The study included people across PD-L1 groups; this NCCP regimen has its own PD-L1 eligibility requirement. Discuss expected benefit, side effects and alternatives for your situation.

questions.q: Is this more chemotherapy?
questions.a: Durvalumab is an immunotherapy infusion. It follows the completed chemotherapy and radiation course and works by changing immune signalling.

questions.q: How long will I receive it?
questions.a: Durvalumab is infused on Day 1 of each 28-day cycle. The course lasts up to 12 months (13 cycles), and can finish earlier if the cancer progresses or side effects make continuation unsuitable. The first dose should start within 42 days after chemoradiotherapy finishes.

questions.q: Why report a cough after chest radiotherapy?
questions.a: Radiation effects, immune inflammation, infection and cancer can look alike. The team needs to assess new or worsening symptoms rather than assume their cause.

questions.q: Will I need routine steroids before each infusion?
questions.a: No routine premedication is specified for this regimen. Steroids may be prescribed to treat particular immune side effects, with a supervised dose and taper.

questions.q: Can side effects happen after I stop?
questions.a: Immune side effects may start during treatment or after the last dose. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and tell every treating clinician that you have received durvalumab, even during a treatment break or after finishing.

rationale.summary: Durvalumab is given after definitive chemoradiotherapy to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning or worsening and improve the chance of longer survival. This is part of a treatment pathway that aims for long-term control and possible cure; it cannot guarantee cure.
rationale.setting: Consolidation for unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with no cancer progression and tumour PD-L1 of at least 1%.
rationale.line: Consolidation after definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy in a curative-intent stage III pathway; not metastatic first-line monotherapy.
factors: Confirm NCCP eligibility, PD-L1 testing, performance status, CRT details and recovery.
Balance durable control and survival evidence against post-radiation lung risk, immune adverse events, pre-existing disease and patient preferences.
Agree route, interval, maximum duration, test ownership, emergency contact and access/reimbursement.
alternatives: Individual alternatives, observation or another treatment pathway require multidisciplinary review of stage, biomarkers, CRT recovery, comorbidity and patient preferences; no cross-trial ranking is implied.
limitations: These NCCP codes cover post-concurrent-CRT consolidation for unresectable stage III NSCLC. They do not cover sequential CRT, resectable perioperative NSCLC, metastatic combination treatment or small-cell lung cancer, even though EMA lists other durvalumab indications.

Current NCCP eligibility requires PD-L1 ≥1%, ECOG 0–1, at least two concurrent platinum cycles, radiation ≥60 Gy, and no progression. PACIFIC enrolled irrespective of PD-L1; overall-trial results are not a PD-L1 ≥1% subgroup estimate.

PD-L1 subgroup analyses were exploratory/post hoc for the 1% threshold, with tissue unavailable for some patients and small subgroups. They cannot establish benefit or no benefit for an individual or replace NCCP eligibility.

PACIFIC studied durvalumab every two weeks. The every-four-week schedule is supported by regulatory drug-exposure bridging; PACIFIC did not directly compare these two schedules or test this fixed dose as its randomised treatment.

For body weight ≤30 kg, NCCP requires 10 mg/kg every two weeks OR 20 mg/kg every four weeks until weight is >30 kg. The clinician must select and prescribe the interval; the fixed-dose card is not an automatic weight-based calculation.

The numerical OS/PFS results below come from the same exploratory five-year update with data cutoff 11 January 2021. They are not mixed with the original co-primary endpoint analyses or presented as individual benefit.
NCCP Table 1 explicitly uses CTCAE 4.03. Confirm the event-specific grade and alternative causes; general interface CTCAE5 aids are not a substitute for this source standard.

Current source hepatitis rows hold AST/ALT >3 through ≤10×ULN; the merged table cell includes >5–10. Stop above 10×ULN, bilirubin >3×ULN, or concurrent AST/ALT >3 and bilirubin >2 without an alternative cause. Do not copy another checkpoint inhibitor’s threshold.

General restart criteria require recovery to grade ≤1, steroid dose ≤10 mg/day prednisone equivalent and resumption within 12 weeks. Organ-specific permanent-stop rules take precedence. Controlled hormone-replacement endocrinopathies have a stated exception to the general severe/recurrent immune-event stop rule.
No durvalumab dose-reduction ladder is recommended for toxicity. Mild/moderate baseline renal or hepatic impairment requires no dose adjustment; data in severe impairment are limited.

Regular endocrine and organ-function monitoring is required; the NCCP source does not prescribe a routine trastuzumab-style cardiac imaging schedule. New cardiac symptoms require targeted urgent assessment.
Omitted inputs remain unassessed; a reassuring single domain does not authorise treatment. Source reconciliation and software checks are not independent consultant/pharmacy approval.

clinical.component_rationale: Durvalumab binds PD-L1 and blocks its interaction with PD-1/CD80, supporting antitumour immune activity. It is given after the completed definitive concurrent CRT phase; its toxicity rules do not assess the earlier cytotoxic or radiation treatment.
key_points: Consolidation for unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with no cancer progression and tumour PD-L1 of at least 1%.

Durvalumab is infused on Day 1 of each 28-day cycle. The course lasts up to 12 months (13 cycles), and can finish earlier if the cancer progresses or side effects make continuation unsuitable. The first dose should start within 42 days after chemoradiotherapy finishes.

The usual reference dose is 1500 mg, given into a vein over about 60 minutes every 28 days. Allow extra time for the clinical review, tests and preparation. If body weight is 30 kg or less, the team must prescribe an appropriate weight-based dose and interval instead of the fixed 1500 mg dose.
Dose escalation/reduction is not recommended for toxicity; use hold/discontinue rules and specialist management.
New pulmonary symptoms after CRT require distinction among radiation pneumonitis, immune pneumonitis, infection and progression.
Source Table 1 is CTCAE4.03; stable treated hypothyroidism/type1 diabetes does not share the blanket hold rule for unstable hyperthyroid/adrenal/pituitary disease.

important_cautions: Review CRT pneumonitis, autoimmune/IBD history, immunodeficiency, transplant, previous immunotherapy/irAEs, infection, systemic immunosuppression and reproductive considerations.
Check weight: at ≤30 kg, fixed 1500 mg must be replaced with a separately prescribed weight-based regimen and chosen interval.

support_summary: Immune side effects may start during treatment or after the last dose. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and tell every treating clinician that you have received durvalumab, even during a treatment break or after finishing.

Radiation inflammation, immune inflammation, infection and cancer can cause similar symptoms. Report new or worsening breathing symptoms promptly so the team can assess the cause. Do not assume a new cough is only an old radiotherapy effect.

Durvalumab alone has minimal sickness risk and no routine premedication is specified. Use anti-sickness or other medicines only as prescribed. Steroids for an immune reaction are a treatment plan supervised by the team, not routine premedication; do not start, reduce or stop them yourself.

Thyroid, adrenal or diabetes problems may need hormone replacement or insulin, sometimes long term. Keep taking prescribed medicines and attend blood tests even when you feel well. Sudden severe weakness, vomiting, faintness, unusual thirst or drowsiness need urgent advice.

Durvalumab is not recommended during pregnancy. The team must help decide whether breastfeeding or durvalumab should be stopped or avoided, weighing the benefits and risks.
baseline: Confirm adult stage III unresectable NSCLC, validated PD-L1 ≥1%, no progression after ≥2 cycles of concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiation ≥60 Gy; ECOG 0–1.
Confirm the CRT completion-to-first-dose interval (≤42 days), plan maximum 12 months and the correct q14/q28 schedule.
FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose, thyroid function; HBsAg, HBcoreAb and hepatitis C screening.
Review CRT pneumonitis, autoimmune/IBD history, immunodeficiency, transplant, previous immunotherapy/irAEs, infection, systemic immunosuppression and reproductive considerations.
Check weight: at ≤30 kg, fixed 1500 mg must be replaced with a separately prescribed weight-based regimen and chosen interval.
before_each_cycle: Review current symptoms, new medicines/steroids, previous immune events, treatment holds and source course duration.
Review available regular FBC, renal/liver, glucose and thyroid results according to the local testing plan; NCCP calls these regular tests without a fixed universal interval.
Assess new/worsening respiratory symptoms before dosing; arrange imaging and differential diagnosis as indicated.
ongoing: Continue regular thyroid, glucose and organ-function monitoring; targeted cortisol/ACTH or other testing follows clinical suspicion and specialist advice.
Cancer response assessment and scans follow the consultant treatment plan.

During an immune hold, investigate other causes; after recovery, steroids usually taper over at least one month. General restart within12 weeks requires grade≤1 and prednisone equivalent≤10 mg/day; organ-specific permanent stops and controlled-endocrine exceptions remain distinct.
Continue immune-effect awareness after completion; endocrine replacement can be prolonged. No routine serial HER2-treatment cardiac schedule is inferred.
access: 60-minute IV infusion in 250mL sodium chloride0.9%, low-protein-binding0.2–0.22micrometre inline filter; final concentration1–15mg/mL.
Do not co-administer other medicines through the same infusion line; resuscitation/anaphylaxis facilities must be available.

patient.title: Nivolumab, ipilimumab, pemetrexed and carboplatin
patient.purpose: This treatment aims to control metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer, help symptoms and extend life. It is usually given without an expectation of cure. The team checks the cancer subtype, molecular results, your health and your preferences before recommending this particular chemotherapy backbone.

agents.name: Nivolumab
agents.explanation: Nivolumab binds PD-1 on T cells. It prevents signals that can reduce the immune attack on cancer. This can also let immune cells inflame healthy tissues. It is infused every 21 days in this plan.
agents.watch: New breathing, bowel, skin, hormone or other symptoms need prompt advice during or after treatment.

agents.name: Ipilimumab
agents.explanation: Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, another control on T-cell activity. It works alongside nivolumab through a different immune checkpoint. It is given every 42 days, so it is absent from each Day 22 visit. Healthy organs can also become inflamed.
agents.watch: Report diarrhoea, tummy pain, rash, severe tiredness, headache or other new symptoms promptly. Keep your immune alert card.
risks: Immune bowel, liver, skin and hormone inflammation

agents.name: Pemetrexed
agents.explanation: Pemetrexed blocks enzymes needed to make DNA and RNA building blocks. Dividing cancer cells are affected, but healthy blood-forming and mouth-lining cells can also be injured. Prescribed folic acid and B12 reduce toxicity; do not omit them because pemetrexed is an antifolate. There are two planned doses in this regimen.
agents.watch: Low blood counts, sore mouth, rash, sickness and kidney problems can occur.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that hinder copying and repair. Healthy tissues can also be harmed. Its dose depends on target exposure (AUC) and measured or estimated kidney function; AUC is not a fixed number of milligrams. There are two planned doses in this regimen.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, nausea, hearing changes or numbness. Tell the nurse immediately about possible allergy during the infusion.

phases.label: Cycle 1 · chemotherapy on Days 1 and 22
phases.detail: The first cycle lasts 42 days: all four medicines on Day 1, then nivolumab, pemetrexed and carboplatin on Day 22. Chemotherapy ends after those two visits. From Cycle 2, nivolumab continues on Days 1 and 22 and ipilimumab on Day 1 of each 42-day cycle.

phases.label: Cycle 2 onwards · immune continuation
phases.detail: Nivolumab every 21 days; ipilimumab every 42 days. No further chemotherapy. Immune treatment continues while appropriate until the cancer progresses, side effects require stopping, or up to 24 months without progression. Plans can change after review.

timeline.text: Includes ipilimumab; chemotherapy in Cycle 1 only

day_groups.title: Day 1 visit
day_groups.body: Nivolumab and ipilimumab are due. In Cycle 1, pemetrexed and carboplatin are also due. Checks, preparation and observation add to the infusion time.
day_groups.action: Report symptoms before treatment and confirm your support prescription.

day_groups.title: Between the first and second visits
day_groups.body: Follow the prescribed support plan after chemotherapy. Symptoms can occur at any time; do not use the date to decide they are safe.
day_groups.action: Contact your team for new diarrhoea, breathing changes, fever or sudden illness.

day_groups.title: Day 22 visit · no ipilimumab
day_groups.body: In Cycle 1 this is nivolumab and the second/final chemotherapy administration. In later cycles this is nivolumab only. Blood count, kidney and liver checks remain due.
day_groups.action: Confirm the active medicines and support plan; do not repeat ipilimumab at this visit.

day_groups.title: Before the next 42-day cycle
day_groups.body: After the final pemetrexed, folate continues for 21 days. In immune-only cycles, continue to report symptoms between visits.
day_groups.action: Confirm the next Day 1 appointment and glucose/thyroid as well as usual blood checks.

support.title: Cycle 1 Days 1 and 22 · chemotherapy-containing visits
support.text: Use dedicated carboplatin AUC ≥4 NCIS row; no routine olanzapine in that row. Folic acid starts before pemetrexed, continues through both chemotherapy visits and for 21 days after the last pemetrexed dose. B12 is given in the preceding week. The source repeats B12 every three cycles if pemetrexed continues; this planned course has only two pemetrexed administrations, so do not automatically continue B12 in immune-only cycles. Your team reconciles the steroid used to prevent pemetrexed rash with the anti-sickness steroid into one clear prescription. Do not add the two schedules together or use leftover steroids yourself. Nivolumab and ipilimumab can inflame healthy organs. Report new symptoms promptly, including after treatment stops; follow-up vigilance is required for at least five months after the last dose.

support.title: Cycle 2 onwards Day 1 · nivolumab + ipilimumab every 42 days
support.text: Ipilimumab is low risk and nivolumab minimal; this combined visit is low risk. No further pemetrexed or platinum: stop/review induction antiemetics and rash steroid; complete the folate tail only. Continue immune symptom education, bloods each treatment and glucose/TFT each 42-day cycle.

support.title: Cycle 2 onwards Day 22 · nivolumab alone, between ipilimumab visits
support.text: No routine prophylactic antiemetic course for nivolumab-only minimal-risk treatment; prescribe symptom-directed rescue under local policy if needed. Ipilimumab is due at the next 42-day cycle Day 1, not every nivolumab visit. Immune toxicity can still occur between ipilimumab visits; the joint hold rule remains relevant.

questions.q: Will chemotherapy continue for months?
questions.a: The planned pemetrexed/platinum course is two administrations, on Days 1 and 22 of Cycle 1. Immune treatment can continue afterwards with a different support plan.

questions.q: Why is ipilimumab absent from some visits?
questions.a: Nivolumab is every 21 days; ipilimumab every 42 days. Day 22 has no ipilimumab. A withheld immune dose is a separate safety decision requiring team review.

questions.q: How will we know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Ask about the goals, scan plan and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping. Side effects do not reliably show treatment response.

questions.q: Can I decide from this guide whether treatment is safe today?
questions.a: No. Your team must interpret symptoms, bloods, previous reactions and the current prescribing protocol. Omitted results are not presumed normal.

questions.q: What if I miss folic acid or a steroid dose?
questions.a: Contact your treatment team or pharmacy for an individual plan. Do not double doses or combine separate steroid schedules yourself.

questions.q: Which risks continue after treatment?
questions.a: Nivolumab and ipilimumab can inflame healthy organs. Report new symptoms promptly, including after treatment stops; follow-up vigilance is required for at least five months after the last dose. Ask about follow-up for any lasting nerve, hearing, kidney, hormone or other problems.

chapters.title: Why this combination is offered
chapters.intro: This treatment aims to control metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer, help symptoms and extend life. It is usually given without an expectation of cure. The team checks the cancer subtype, molecular results, your health and your preferences before recommending this particular chemotherapy backbone.

items.title: What do the cancer terms mean?
items.text: Metastatic means cancer has spread beyond where it started. NSCLC is a broad lung-cancer group; non-squamous describes one histology, often adenocarcinoma. First-line means the first systemic treatment for this setting. The pathology and molecular results help determine whether this exact pemetrexed combination suits your cancer.

items.title: What does the evidence mean for me?
items.text: In CheckMate 9LA, the strategy of two immune medicines with a short chemotherapy course helped people live longer than chemotherapy alone. The study included different histologies and platinum medicines. It cannot tell exactly what benefit you will have, or prove that this particular platinum is better for you.

items.title: What are the alternatives?
items.text: Ask how tumour tests, fitness and your priorities affect the options, including other drug combinations, targeted treatment when relevant, a clinical trial or symptom-focused care. Support for breathlessness, pain, appetite and emotional concerns can accompany anticancer treatment.

chapters.title: Before the first visit
chapters.intro: The preventive medicines and baseline review are part of the treatment.

items.title: Describe your usual health
items.text: Tell the team about your usual breathing and bowel pattern, autoimmune illness, lung inflammation, infections, nerve or hearing symptoms, diabetes, and all prescription or non-prescription medicines. This helps identify a new problem promptly.

items.title: Folate, B12 and steroid plan
items.text: Folic acid starts before pemetrexed, continues through both chemotherapy visits and for 21 days after the last pemetrexed dose. B12 is given in the preceding week. The source repeats B12 every three cycles if pemetrexed continues; this planned course has only two pemetrexed administrations, so do not automatically continue B12 in immune-only cycles. Your team reconciles the steroid used to prevent pemetrexed rash with the anti-sickness steroid into one clear prescription. Do not add the two schedules together or use leftover steroids yourself.

items.title: Prepare contact and practical support
items.text: Keep your oncology and out-of-hours instructions, a thermometer, treatment names and immune alert card available. Arrange blood tests, transport and help at home where needed. Ask what to do if a support medicine is missed; do not double a dose without advice.

chapters.title: Two chemotherapy visits, then continuing immunotherapy
chapters.intro: The first cycle lasts 42 days: all four medicines on Day 1, then nivolumab, pemetrexed and carboplatin on Day 22. Chemotherapy ends after those two visits. From Cycle 2, nivolumab continues on Days 1 and 22 and ipilimumab on Day 1 of each 42-day cycle.

items.title: Day 1 and Day 22 differ
items.text: Cycle 1 Day 1 includes all four medicines. Day 22 is three weeks later and includes nivolumab plus the second and final planned chemotherapy doses, but no ipilimumab. A 42-day cycle is six weeks.

items.title: The next 42-day cycles
items.text: From Cycle 2, Day 1 includes nivolumab and ipilimumab. Day 22 includes nivolumab only. No pemetrexed or platinum is planned in this continuation phase. The support medicines change too; check the updated prescription.

items.title: How long does treatment last?
items.text: Immune treatment continues while appropriate until the cancer progresses, side effects require stopping, or up to 24 months without progression. Plans can change after review. The team reviews benefit, symptoms and scans. A delay can allow investigation or recovery. It does not mean you have failed treatment.

chapters.title: What the checks are looking for
chapters.intro: Different checks assess safety today, possible toxicity and cancer response.

items.title: Blood count, kidney and liver
items.text: Blood counts and kidney/liver tests are checked before each Day 1 and Day 22 treatment. Blood counts show infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets. Kidney results influence chemotherapy safety. Normal results from a previous visit do not rule out a new problem.

items.title: Hormones and immune effects
items.text: Glucose and thyroid tests are checked before each 42-day cycle. The baseline assessment includes morning cortisol and hepatitis tests. New symptoms can require extra tests between planned visits; routine blood tests alone cannot exclude all immune side effects.

items.title: Scans and decisions
items.text: Your consultant sets the scan schedule. The team considers symptoms, examination, results and what matters to you. Side effects are not a reliable measure of how well treatment is controlling cancer.

chapters.title: Effects around the chemotherapy visits
chapters.intro: These are selected possibilities, not a forecast or a complete medicine leaflet.

items.title: Sickness, appetite and constipation
items.text: Take preventive anti-sickness medicines as prescribed. Tell the team if they do not control symptoms. Persistent vomiting, difficulty keeping fluids down or much less urine need prompt advice. Some anti-sickness and pain medicines cause constipation; ask for a bowel plan.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell need immediate oncology advice, even with a normal temperature. Counts can fall between visits and cannot be judged from the calendar. Report unexpected bruising, bleeding or worsening breathlessness.

items.title: Mouth, skin and tiredness
items.text: Use gentle mouth care and report ulcers, painful swallowing, rash or reduced intake. Balance rest with manageable activity. Marked or sudden weakness needs assessment: fatigue can also be caused by infection, anaemia or immune hormone problems.

items.title: Kidneys, hearing and nerves
items.text: Carboplatin dosing depends on kidney function. Tell the team about reduced urine, new ringing in the ears, hearing loss, tingling or numbness before another chemotherapy dose.

chapters.title: Immune effects need early reporting
chapters.intro: Nivolumab and ipilimumab can inflame healthy organs. Report new symptoms promptly, including after treatment stops; follow-up vigilance is required for at least five months after the last dose.

items.title: Breathing, bowel, skin and urine
items.text: New cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, blood or mucus in stool, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, dark urine, reduced urine or swelling need prompt assessment. Do not assume these are ordinary chemotherapy effects. Blistering or peeling skin or sores in the eyes or mouth need urgent care.

items.title: Hormones, heart, muscles and nerves
items.text: Report unusual weakness, persistent headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, palpitations, muscle weakness or vision changes. Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion or major breathing difficulty needs emergency care. Some hormone effects require long-term replacement.

items.title: Treatment may need to pause
items.text: The team may withhold both immune medicines, investigate and prescribe steroids or other treatment. This is different from the short preventive steroid course around chemotherapy. Do not start leftover steroids, change their dose or abruptly stop a prescribed course.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: The aim is to fit care around the things that matter to you.

items.title: Food, fluids, work and movement
items.text: Ask for help with weight loss, reduced appetite, work adjustments, transport or household tasks. A fixed fluid target is not suitable for everyone. Do not drive if dizzy, very tired or affected by sedating medicines; cisplatin anti-sickness treatment can include olanzapine.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility before treatment where relevant. Ask for a written contraception plan covering all four medicines and the period after treatment. Report possible pregnancy promptly and do not breastfeed unless your team confirms it is safe.

items.title: Support and choices
items.text: Ask for an interpreter, accessible information, psychological support or a trusted person to join appointments. Discuss alternatives, expected benefits and lasting harms. You can revisit your preferences as treatment continues.

chapters.title: Care after a drug stops
chapters.intro: Stopping chemotherapy or immunotherapy changes the plan but does not immediately remove all risks.

items.title: After the second pemetrexed dose
items.text: Finish the prescribed 21-day folic-acid tail after the last pemetrexed. Review anti-sickness and rash-steroid stop dates. B12 is not automatically continued just because immune therapy continues.

items.title: After the last immune dose
items.text: Nivolumab and ipilimumab can inflame healthy organs. Report new symptoms promptly, including after treatment stops; follow-up vigilance is required for at least five months after the last dose. Keep the alert card and tell other healthcare professionals about both immune medicines. Ask who will arrange follow-up and review any unresolved symptoms.

items.title: Use your team’s urgent instructions
items.text: When you call, state your treatment names, last treatment date, what changed, temperature if known, and whether you can drink and pass urine. Do not delay calling while gathering every detail.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: The combined strategy improved survival compared with chemotherapy in the trial population, with some durable responses. Benefits and harms vary between people.
evidence.interpretation: The study tested the combined strategy across different lung-cancer histologies and chemotherapy choices. Your own expected benefit depends on your cancer and health.
evidence.population: Previously untreated metastatic/recurrent NSCLC without sensitising EGFR/ALK alterations.
evidence.limitations: This is not a personal survival forecast or a direct comparison of carboplatin with cisplatin.

rationale.summary: Nivolumab blocks PD-1 and ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, supporting T-cell antitumour activity through different checkpoint pathways. Pemetrexed inhibits nucleotide synthesis and carboplatin damages DNA. The trial combines limited initial chemotherapy with continuing dual immunotherapy; this rationale does not predict individual response.
rationale.setting: First-line metastatic NSCLC; histology-appropriate pemetrexed backbone
factors: Confirm first-line metastatic/recurrent NSCLC, no sensitising EGFR mutation or ALK translocation, ECOG 0–1 and pemetrexed suitability for the histology. Current NCCP wording removed non-squamous; this is not permission to use pemetrexed for every histology.

FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose, thyroid function, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C RNA and morning cortisol. Measured isotope GFR is preferred for carboplatin; review method, recency and Calvert dose.

Review significant autoimmune disease, systemic immunosuppression, infection, CNS disease, prior PD-1/PD-L1 treatment, ILD, hearing/tinnitus and neuropathy. Audiology/CrCl if indicated. Confirm folate lead-in and B12.
alternatives: The consultant compares biomarker-directed therapy when appropriate, other immune/chemotherapy options, trials and symptom-focused care in the context of molecular results, fitness and preferences. Supportive/palliative care can accompany anticancer treatment.
limitations: NCCP cycles are 42 days. The trial description of two chemotherapy cycles refers to two 21-day chemotherapy administrations, not two 42-day cycles.
Checkpoint doses are held or stopped, not reduced. If either nivolumab or ipilimumab is withheld, the other is also withheld; any later nivolumab-only plan is a consultant decision.
Current NCCP Table 1 uses CTCAE v4: grade 3 colitis stops both immune drugs, whereas grade 3 creatinine elevation holds them. Do not import another checkpoint regimen’s thresholds.
Chemotherapy-specific modifications cease when chemotherapy ends; ongoing low counts or organ dysfunction still require clinical assessment.

evidence.population: 719 previously untreated adults with stage IV/recurrent NSCLC without sensitising EGFR/ALK alterations; mixed squamous and non-squamous histologies.
evidence.comparison: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab and two cycles of histology-based platinum-doublet chemotherapy (361) versus four chemotherapy cycles (358); optional pemetrexed maintenance in the control non-squamous population.
evidence.applicability: Supports the overall first-line strategy. The pemetrexed protocols correspond to the non-squamous chemotherapy backbone studied; overall results pool histologies and platinum choices. No separate randomized benefit estimate for this exact carboplatin backbone is asserted.

endpoints.metric: Overall randomized population, final six-year analysis
endpoints.result_text: HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.63–0.87); six-year survival 16% versus 10%, minimum follow-up 68.6 months.
endpoints.interpretation: Population-level randomized comparison of the complete treatment strategies, not a personal survival prediction or a cisplatin-versus-carboplatin comparison.

sources.label: Carbone et al., ESMO Open 2025

endpoints.interpretation: Descriptive subgroup result; does not isolate pemetrexed/carboplatin from pemetrexed/cisplatin or establish comparative benefit between platinum choices.
endpoints.analysis_status: Final follow-up subgroup analysis; retain subgroup limitations.

sources.label: CheckMate 9LA final six-year report

evidence.qualitative_result: The combined strategy improved survival compared with chemotherapy in the trial population, with some durable responses. Benefits and harms vary between people.
limitations: The whole-trial result includes squamous and non-squamous disease and different chemotherapy backbones.
Non-squamous subgroup data do not establish a separate survival effect for carboplatin versus cisplatin.
Trial participants and treatment selection differ from an individual patient; the reported survival proportions are not individual benefit predictions.
The current NCCP broad NSCLC wording must not be treated as evidence for a histologically inappropriate pemetrexed backbone.

sources.label: CheckMate 9LA final six-year randomized-trial report

evidence.harms: Combining chemotherapy with dual checkpoint blockade introduces cytotoxic and immune-mediated harms; important inflammation can affect multiple organs and require hospital care or permanent treatment cessation. Final follow-up reported no new safety signals; this does not imply no risk.

patient.title: Nivolumab, ipilimumab, pemetrexed and cisplatin
patient.purpose: This treatment aims to control metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer, help symptoms and extend life. It is usually given without an expectation of cure. The team checks the cancer subtype, molecular results, your health and your preferences before recommending this particular chemotherapy backbone.

agents.name: Nivolumab
agents.explanation: Nivolumab binds PD-1 on T cells. It prevents signals that can reduce the immune attack on cancer. This can also let immune cells inflame healthy tissues. It is infused every 21 days in this plan.
agents.watch: New breathing, bowel, skin, hormone or other symptoms need prompt advice during or after treatment.

agents.name: Ipilimumab
agents.explanation: Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, another control on T-cell activity. It works alongside nivolumab through a different immune checkpoint. It is given every 42 days, so it is absent from each Day 22 visit. Healthy organs can also become inflamed.
agents.watch: Report diarrhoea, tummy pain, rash, severe tiredness, headache or other new symptoms promptly. Keep your immune alert card.
risks: Immune bowel, liver, skin and hormone inflammation

agents.name: Pemetrexed
agents.explanation: Pemetrexed blocks enzymes needed to make DNA and RNA building blocks. Dividing cancer cells are affected, but healthy blood-forming and mouth-lining cells can also be injured. Prescribed folic acid and B12 reduce toxicity; do not omit them because pemetrexed is an antifolate. There are two planned doses in this regimen.
agents.watch: Low blood counts, sore mouth, rash, sickness and kidney problems can occur.

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that hinder copying and repair. Healthy tissues can also be harmed. Kidney injury, changes in salts in the blood, hearing damage and nerve symptoms are important risks. Extra fluids and electrolyte checks are part of treatment. There are two planned doses in this regimen.
agents.watch: Report reduced urine, vomiting, ringing in the ears, hearing change or numbness. Hydration instructions are individual.

phases.detail: Nivolumab every 21 days; ipilimumab every 42 days. No further chemotherapy. Immune treatment continues while appropriate until the cancer progresses, side effects require stopping, or up to 24 months without progression. Plans can change after review.

questions.q: Will chemotherapy continue for months?
questions.a: The planned pemetrexed/platinum course is two administrations, on Days 1 and 22 of Cycle 1. Immune treatment can continue afterwards with a different support plan.

questions.q: Why is ipilimumab absent from some visits?
questions.a: Nivolumab is every 21 days; ipilimumab every 42 days. Day 22 has no ipilimumab. A withheld immune dose is a separate safety decision requiring team review.

questions.q: How will we know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Ask about the goals, scan plan and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping. Side effects do not reliably show treatment response.

questions.q: Can I decide from this guide whether treatment is safe today?
questions.a: No. Your team must interpret symptoms, bloods, previous reactions and the current prescribing protocol. Omitted results are not presumed normal.

questions.q: What if I miss folic acid or a steroid dose?
questions.a: Contact your treatment team or pharmacy for an individual plan. Do not double doses or combine separate steroid schedules yourself.

questions.q: Which risks continue after treatment?
questions.a: Nivolumab and ipilimumab can inflame healthy organs. Report new symptoms promptly, including after treatment stops; follow-up vigilance is required for at least five months after the last dose. Ask about follow-up for any lasting nerve, hearing, kidney, hormone or other problems.

chapters.title: Why this combination is offered
chapters.intro: This treatment aims to control metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer, help symptoms and extend life. It is usually given without an expectation of cure. The team checks the cancer subtype, molecular results, your health and your preferences before recommending this particular chemotherapy backbone.

items.title: What do the cancer terms mean?
items.text: Metastatic means cancer has spread beyond where it started. NSCLC is a broad lung-cancer group; non-squamous describes one histology, often adenocarcinoma. First-line means the first systemic treatment for this setting. The pathology and molecular results help determine whether this exact pemetrexed combination suits your cancer.

items.title: What does the evidence mean for me?
items.text: In CheckMate 9LA, the strategy of two immune medicines with a short chemotherapy course helped people live longer than chemotherapy alone. The study included different histologies and platinum medicines. It cannot tell exactly what benefit you will have, or prove that this particular platinum is better for you.

items.title: What are the alternatives?
items.text: Ask how tumour tests, fitness and your priorities affect the options, including other drug combinations, targeted treatment when relevant, a clinical trial or symptom-focused care. Support for breathlessness, pain, appetite and emotional concerns can accompany anticancer treatment.

chapters.title: Before the first visit
chapters.intro: The preventive medicines and baseline review are part of the treatment.

items.title: Describe your usual health
items.text: Tell the team about your usual breathing and bowel pattern, autoimmune illness, lung inflammation, infections, nerve or hearing symptoms, diabetes, and all prescription or non-prescription medicines. This helps identify a new problem promptly.

items.title: Folate, B12 and steroid plan
items.text: Folic acid starts before pemetrexed, continues through both chemotherapy visits and for 21 days after the last pemetrexed dose. B12 is given in the preceding week. The source repeats B12 every three cycles if pemetrexed continues; this planned course has only two pemetrexed administrations, so do not automatically continue B12 in immune-only cycles. Your team reconciles the steroid used to prevent pemetrexed rash with the anti-sickness steroid into one clear prescription. Do not add the two schedules together or use leftover steroids yourself.

items.title: Prepare contact and practical support
items.text: Keep your oncology and out-of-hours instructions, a thermometer, treatment names and immune alert card available. Arrange blood tests, transport and help at home where needed. Ask what to do if a support medicine is missed; do not double a dose without advice.

chapters.title: Two chemotherapy visits, then continuing immunotherapy
chapters.intro: The first cycle lasts 42 days: all four medicines on Day 1, then nivolumab, pemetrexed and cisplatin on Day 22. Chemotherapy ends after those two visits. From Cycle 2, nivolumab continues on Days 1 and 22 and ipilimumab on Day 1 of each 42-day cycle.

items.title: Day 1 and Day 22 differ
items.text: Cycle 1 Day 1 includes all four medicines. Day 22 is three weeks later and includes nivolumab plus the second and final planned chemotherapy doses, but no ipilimumab. A 42-day cycle is six weeks.

items.title: The next 42-day cycles
items.text: From Cycle 2, Day 1 includes nivolumab and ipilimumab. Day 22 includes nivolumab only. No pemetrexed or platinum is planned in this continuation phase. The support medicines change too; check the updated prescription.

items.title: How long does treatment last?
items.text: Immune treatment continues while appropriate until the cancer progresses, side effects require stopping, or up to 24 months without progression. Plans can change after review. The team reviews benefit, symptoms and scans. A delay can allow investigation or recovery. It does not mean you have failed treatment.

chapters.title: What the checks are looking for
chapters.intro: Different checks assess safety today, possible toxicity and cancer response.

items.title: Blood count, kidney and liver
items.text: Blood counts and kidney/liver tests are checked before each Day 1 and Day 22 treatment. Blood counts show infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets. Kidney results influence chemotherapy safety. Normal results from a previous visit do not rule out a new problem.

items.title: Hormones and immune effects
items.text: Glucose and thyroid tests are checked before each 42-day cycle. The baseline assessment includes morning cortisol and hepatitis tests. New symptoms can require extra tests between planned visits; routine blood tests alone cannot exclude all immune side effects.

items.title: Scans and decisions
items.text: Your consultant sets the scan schedule. The team considers symptoms, examination, results and what matters to you. Side effects are not a reliable measure of how well treatment is controlling cancer.

chapters.title: Effects around the chemotherapy visits
chapters.intro: These are selected possibilities, not a forecast or a complete medicine leaflet.

items.title: Sickness, appetite and constipation
items.text: Take preventive anti-sickness medicines as prescribed. Tell the team if they do not control symptoms. Persistent vomiting, difficulty keeping fluids down or much less urine need prompt advice. Some anti-sickness and pain medicines cause constipation; ask for a bowel plan.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell need immediate oncology advice, even with a normal temperature. Counts can fall between visits and cannot be judged from the calendar. Report unexpected bruising, bleeding or worsening breathlessness.

items.title: Mouth, skin and tiredness
items.text: Use gentle mouth care and report ulcers, painful swallowing, rash or reduced intake. Balance rest with manageable activity. Marked or sudden weakness needs assessment: fatigue can also be caused by infection, anaemia or immune hormone problems.

items.title: Kidneys, hearing and nerves
items.text: Cisplatin can injure kidneys and affect blood salts, hearing and nerves. Fluids before and after the infusion reduce particular risks, and your fluid advice is individual. Tell the team about reduced urine, new ringing in the ears, hearing loss, tingling or numbness before another chemotherapy dose.

chapters.title: Immune effects need early reporting
chapters.intro: Nivolumab and ipilimumab can inflame healthy organs. Report new symptoms promptly, including after treatment stops; follow-up vigilance is required for at least five months after the last dose.

items.title: Breathing, bowel, skin and urine
items.text: New cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, blood or mucus in stool, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, dark urine, reduced urine or swelling need prompt assessment. Do not assume these are ordinary chemotherapy effects. Blistering or peeling skin or sores in the eyes or mouth need urgent care.

items.title: Hormones, heart, muscles and nerves
items.text: Report unusual weakness, persistent headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, palpitations, muscle weakness or vision changes. Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion or major breathing difficulty needs emergency care. Some hormone effects require long-term replacement.

items.title: Treatment may need to pause
items.text: The team may withhold both immune medicines, investigate and prescribe steroids or other treatment. This is different from the short preventive steroid course around chemotherapy. Do not start leftover steroids, change their dose or abruptly stop a prescribed course.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: The aim is to fit care around the things that matter to you.

items.title: Food, fluids, work and movement
items.text: Ask for help with weight loss, reduced appetite, work adjustments, transport or household tasks. A fixed fluid target is not suitable for everyone. Do not drive if dizzy, very tired or affected by sedating medicines; cisplatin anti-sickness treatment can include olanzapine.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility before treatment where relevant. Ask for a written contraception plan covering all four medicines and the period after treatment. Report possible pregnancy promptly and do not breastfeed unless your team confirms it is safe.

items.title: Support and choices
items.text: Ask for an interpreter, accessible information, psychological support or a trusted person to join appointments. Discuss alternatives, expected benefits and lasting harms. You can revisit your preferences as treatment continues.

chapters.title: Care after a drug stops
chapters.intro: Stopping chemotherapy or immunotherapy changes the plan but does not immediately remove all risks.

items.title: After the second pemetrexed dose
items.text: Finish the prescribed 21-day folic-acid tail after the last pemetrexed. Review anti-sickness and rash-steroid stop dates. B12 is not automatically continued just because immune therapy continues.

items.title: After the last immune dose
items.text: Nivolumab and ipilimumab can inflame healthy organs. Report new symptoms promptly, including after treatment stops; follow-up vigilance is required for at least five months after the last dose. Keep the alert card and tell other healthcare professionals about both immune medicines. Ask who will arrange follow-up and review any unresolved symptoms.

items.title: Use your team’s urgent instructions
items.text: When you call, state your treatment names, last treatment date, what changed, temperature if known, and whether you can drink and pass urine. Do not delay calling while gathering every detail.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: The combined strategy improved survival compared with chemotherapy in the trial population, with some durable responses. Benefits and harms vary between people.
evidence.interpretation: The study tested the combined strategy across different lung-cancer histologies and chemotherapy choices. Your own expected benefit depends on your cancer and health.
evidence.population: Previously untreated metastatic/recurrent NSCLC without sensitising EGFR/ALK alterations.
evidence.limitations: This is not a personal survival forecast or a direct comparison of carboplatin with cisplatin.

patient.indication_text: First-line metastatic NSCLC in adults without a sensitising EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. Current NCCP wording is histology-broad; the suitability of this pemetrexed backbone still requires explicit histology review.

Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion or major breathing difficulty needs emergency care.

rationale.summary: Nivolumab blocks PD-1 and ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, supporting T-cell antitumour activity through different checkpoint pathways. Pemetrexed inhibits nucleotide synthesis and cisplatin damages DNA. The trial combines limited initial chemotherapy with continuing dual immunotherapy; this rationale does not predict individual response.
rationale.setting: First-line metastatic NSCLC; histology-appropriate pemetrexed backbone
factors: Confirm first-line metastatic/recurrent NSCLC, no sensitising EGFR mutation or ALK translocation, ECOG 0–1 and pemetrexed suitability for the histology. Current NCCP wording removed non-squamous; this is not permission to use pemetrexed for every histology.

FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose, thyroid function, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C RNA and morning cortisol. Assess renal function, fluid status and the cisplatin hydration/electrolyte plan.

Review significant autoimmune disease, systemic immunosuppression, infection, CNS disease, prior PD-1/PD-L1 treatment, ILD, hearing/tinnitus and neuropathy. Audiology/CrCl if indicated. Confirm folate lead-in and B12.
alternatives: The consultant compares biomarker-directed therapy when appropriate, other immune/chemotherapy options, trials and symptom-focused care in the context of molecular results, fitness and preferences. Supportive/palliative care can accompany anticancer treatment.
limitations: NCCP cycles are 42 days. The trial description of two chemotherapy cycles refers to two 21-day chemotherapy administrations, not two 42-day cycles.
Checkpoint doses are held or stopped, not reduced. If either nivolumab or ipilimumab is withheld, the other is also withheld; any later nivolumab-only plan is a consultant decision.
Current NCCP Table 1 uses CTCAE v4: grade 3 colitis stops both immune drugs, whereas grade 3 creatinine elevation holds them. Do not import another checkpoint regimen’s thresholds.
Chemotherapy-specific modifications cease when chemotherapy ends; ongoing low counts or organ dysfunction still require clinical assessment.
At immune-only Day 1, ipilimumab makes the visit low emetic risk; Day 22 is nivolumab alone and minimal risk. Do not carry the high-risk induction support forward automatically.
Your team reconciles the steroid used to prevent pemetrexed rash with the anti-sickness steroid into one clear prescription. Do not add the two schedules together or use leftover steroids yourself.

disease_and_biomarker_context: First-line metastatic NSCLC in adults without a sensitising EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. Current NCCP wording is histology-broad; the suitability of this pemetrexed backbone still requires explicit histology review.
eligibility_orientation: Confirm first-line metastatic/recurrent NSCLC, no sensitising EGFR mutation or ALK translocation, ECOG 0–1 and pemetrexed suitability for the histology. Current NCCP wording removed non-squamous; this is not permission to use pemetrexed for every histology.

FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose, thyroid function, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C RNA and morning cortisol. Assess renal function, fluid status and the cisplatin hydration/electrolyte plan.

Review significant autoimmune disease, systemic immunosuppression, infection, CNS disease, prior PD-1/PD-L1 treatment, ILD, hearing/tinnitus and neuropathy. Audiology/CrCl if indicated. Confirm folate lead-in and B12.

administration: Nivolumab over 30 minutes first; ipilimumab over 30 minutes on Day 1 only; pemetrexed over 10 minutes; cisplatin over 60 minutes, starting 30 minutes after pemetrexed, with pre/post hydration. access: IV treatment through agreed venous access; no home chemotherapy pump.

Arrange transport, lab appointments and prescriptions. Allow extra time for pre/post hydration and review fluid restrictions, urine and electrolyte needs individually. Keep immune alert information available for every healthcare contact.

evidence.population: 719 previously untreated adults with stage IV/recurrent NSCLC without sensitising EGFR/ALK alterations; mixed squamous and non-squamous histologies.
evidence.comparison: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab and two cycles of histology-based platinum-doublet chemotherapy (361) versus four chemotherapy cycles (358); optional pemetrexed maintenance in the control non-squamous population.
evidence.applicability: Supports the overall first-line strategy. The pemetrexed protocols correspond to the non-squamous chemotherapy backbone studied; overall results pool histologies and platinum choices. No separate randomized benefit estimate for this exact cisplatin backbone is asserted.

endpoints.metric: Overall randomized population, final six-year analysis
endpoints.result_text: HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.63–0.87); six-year survival 16% versus 10%, minimum follow-up 68.6 months.
endpoints.interpretation: Population-level randomized comparison of the complete treatment strategies, not a personal survival prediction or a cisplatin-versus-carboplatin comparison.

sources.label: Carbone et al., ESMO Open 2025

endpoints.interpretation: Descriptive subgroup result; does not isolate pemetrexed/carboplatin from pemetrexed/cisplatin or establish comparative benefit between platinum choices.
endpoints.analysis_status: Final follow-up subgroup analysis; retain subgroup limitations.

sources.label: CheckMate 9LA final six-year report

evidence.qualitative_result: The combined strategy improved survival compared with chemotherapy in the trial population, with some durable responses. Benefits and harms vary between people.
limitations: The whole-trial result includes squamous and non-squamous disease and different chemotherapy backbones.
Non-squamous subgroup data do not establish a separate survival effect for carboplatin versus cisplatin.
Trial participants and treatment selection differ from an individual patient; the reported survival proportions are not individual benefit predictions.
The current NCCP broad NSCLC wording must not be treated as evidence for a histologically inappropriate pemetrexed backbone.

sources.label: CheckMate 9LA final six-year randomized-trial report

evidence.harms: Combining chemotherapy with dual checkpoint blockade introduces cytotoxic and immune-mediated harms; important inflammation can affect multiple organs and require hospital care or permanent treatment cessation. Final follow-up reported no new safety signals; this does not imply no risk.

patient.title: Pemetrexed + Cisplatin

agents.name: Pemetrexed
agents.explanation: Pemetrexed blocks several enzymes that use folate to make the building blocks of DNA and RNA. This can slow or stop cancer-cell growth. Healthy cells can also be affected. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce important toxicities and are part of treatment.
agents.watch: Take the prescribed folic acid and attend for B12. Report mouth sores, diarrhoea, a rash, breathlessness or reduced urine; check before taking ibuprofen or other non-prescription medicines.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Skin rash; rarely serious skin reactions

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
agents.watch: Report ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hearing changes or tinnitus, which can persist
Numbness or tingling, which can persist
Electrolyte changes and need for hydration

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Is immunotherapy part of these two medicines?
questions.a: This guide covers pemetrexed and cisplatin chemotherapy. It does not include an immunotherapy medicine. If nivolumab, pembrolizumab or another medicine is also prescribed, obtain its separate regimen, consent, monitoring and emergency instructions. Mesothelioma and NSCLC have different aims and evidence; ask which indication is on your prescription.

questions.q: Will I always have four cycles?
questions.a: For pleural mesothelioma, the source describes up to 4–6 cycles. For advanced non-squamous NSCLC, it describes 4–6 combination cycles followed, when appropriate, by a separate pemetrexed maintenance plan (NCCP00222). The selected preoperative nivolumab combination uses three cycles and a separate immunotherapy plan (NCCP00849). Your team confirms which course applies and may stop or change it earlier.

questions.q: Why take vitamins during chemotherapy?
questions.a: Folic acid and vitamin B12 lower important pemetrexed side effects. They are prescribed parts of this regimen. Tell the team promptly if they were missed.

questions.q: What happens when the platinum chemotherapy stops?
questions.a: The next step depends on your disease and treatment aim. Selected advanced NSCLC plans may move to pemetrexed maintenance under a separate regimen. Preoperative treatment leads to a surgical-team review; mesothelioma follow-up is agreed with the oncology team.

Tell the team promptly about new tinnitus, hearing change, numbness, weakness or difficulty walking.

chapters.title: Understanding your treatment
chapters.intro: The same chemotherapy pair appears in more than one disease setting.

items.title: Confirm the indication
items.text: Pemetrexed + Cisplatin is chemotherapy used for selected people with unresectable pleural mesothelioma or non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer. The aim may be disease control or, within a separate combined preoperative plan, support for surgery. Ask your team to explain the expected benefit for your own diagnosis.

items.title: This guide’s scope
items.text: This guide covers pemetrexed and cisplatin chemotherapy. It does not include an immunotherapy medicine. If nivolumab, pembrolizumab or another medicine is also prescribed, obtain its separate regimen, consent, monitoring and emergency instructions. Mesothelioma and NSCLC have different aims and evidence; ask which indication is on your prescription.

items.title: How long treatment lasts
items.text: For pleural mesothelioma, the source describes up to 4–6 cycles. For advanced non-squamous NSCLC, it describes 4–6 combination cycles followed, when appropriate, by a separate pemetrexed maintenance plan (NCCP00222). The selected preoperative nivolumab combination uses three cycles and a separate immunotherapy plan (NCCP00849). Your team confirms which course applies and may stop or change it earlier.

chapters.title: Before the first treatment
chapters.intro: Preparation reduces avoidable risk and makes the plan clearer.

items.title: Blood tests and kidney assessment
items.text: Baseline checks include full blood count, kidney and liver tests. The team also reviews the cisplatin hydration plan and existing kidney problems.

items.title: Nerves and hearing
items.text: Describe any numbness, weakness, ringing in the ears or hearing difficulty before starting. A hearing test is arranged when clinically indicated.

items.title: Vitamins, steroids and medicines
items.text: Confirm that folic acid has started, B12 was given, and you have one clear steroid and anti-sickness prescription. Bring a complete medicines list.

items.title: Consent and priorities
items.text: Confirm the treatment aim and indication, likely benefit and uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, serious and lasting risks, kidney/hearing/nerve problems, fertility and pregnancy advice, vitamin and steroid plans, and the chance of delays or dose changes.

chapters.title: What happens on treatment day
chapters.intro: The infusion times are only part of your visit.

items.title: Assessment first
items.text: Blood results and symptoms are reviewed before a dose is authorised. A delay or reduction may allow recovery and reduce lasting harm.

items.title: Your infusions
items.text: Pemetrexed is given into a vein over about 10 minutes, followed by cisplatin over about 60 minutes, starting 30 minutes after pemetrexed. Fluids before and after cisplatin make the visit longer; the team individualises hydration and electrolyte replacement. The whole visit also includes blood-result review, prevention medicines, preparation and observation.

items.title: During the infusion
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately about feeling unwell, breathing difficulty, itching, swelling, pain, burning or redness around the drip. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

chapters.title: Looking after yourself between visits
chapters.intro: Ask for help early with symptoms and practical difficulties.

items.title: Symptoms and daily life
items.text: Rest when needed while keeping activity manageable. Ask for nutrition, fatigue, work, transport or financial support. Keep a short symptom record for review.

items.title: Mouth and bowel care
items.text: Follow the team’s mouth-care plan. Report painful swallowing, persistent diarrhoea, vomiting or difficulty maintaining fluids; severe symptoms need urgent advice.

items.title: Hearing and nerves
items.text: Report tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or difficulty with everyday tasks before further treatment. These effects can persist after treatment ends.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation, contraception and pregnancy plans before treatment. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are exclusions in the regimen. Ask the team for the medicine-specific contraception period.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Use your unit’s 24-hour advice number and emergency instructions.

items.title: Possible infection
items.text: Call immediately for the fever threshold your unit gives you, shaking chills or sudden illness. You can have a serious infection without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next appointment.

items.title: Other urgent changes
items.text: Call urgently for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, severe or persistent diarrhoea, inability to drink, very little urine, a spreading or blistering rash, or swelling/wheeze during an infusion. Tell the team promptly about new tinnitus, hearing change, numbness, weakness or difficulty walking.

items.title: When you call
items.text: Give your medicines, last treatment date and symptoms. Explain whether you can drink and pass urine. If emergency help is needed, follow local emergency instructions and tell staff you are receiving chemotherapy.

chapters.title: Review, completion and a possible next phase
chapters.intro: The plan changes according to benefit, recovery and your priorities.

items.title: Response assessment
items.text: Scans and other tests are timed by the consultant’s treatment plan. Symptoms and side effects alone do not show whether treatment is working.

items.title: At a treatment change
items.text: For pleural mesothelioma, the source describes up to 4–6 cycles. For advanced non-squamous NSCLC, it describes 4–6 combination cycles followed, when appropriate, by a separate pemetrexed maintenance plan (NCCP00222). The selected preoperative nivolumab combination uses three cycles and a separate immunotherapy plan (NCCP00849). Your team confirms which course applies and may stop or change it earlier.

items.title: After the last pemetrexed
items.text: Continue folic acid for 21 days after the final dose. Agree follow-up for persistent kidney, blood-count, hearing, nerve or other problems. A maintenance prescription has its own ongoing tests and prevention medicines.

day_groups.body: Continue folic acid and the prescribed anti-sickness medicines. Your team combines the pemetrexed rash steroid and anti-sickness steroid into one clear schedule.
day_groups.action: Do not double up dexamethasone courses. Call if vomiting prevents medicines or fluids staying down.

day_groups.title: Recovery and symptom monitoring
day_groups.body: Fatigue, bowel or mouth symptoms and low blood counts may develop between visits. Nerve or hearing symptoms can build across cycles.
day_groups.action: Use the emergency contact plan at any time; do not wait for the next treatment day.

day_groups.title: Review before the next cycle
day_groups.body: The team checks blood counts, kidney and liver results and symptoms before deciding whether to continue, delay or change a dose.
day_groups.action: Bring your medicine list and symptom notes; confirm the next B12 injection and whether the treatment phase changes.

support.title: Folic acid every day
support.text: The source uses 350–1000 micrograms daily: at least five doses during the seven days before the first pemetrexed, throughout treatment and for 21 days after the last pemetrexed. Follow your own prescription and tell the team about missed doses.

support.title: Vitamin B12 injection
support.text: The source uses 1000 micrograms into a muscle during the week before the first pemetrexed, then every three cycles. Later injections can be on treatment day. Confirm who books them.

support.title: One steroid schedule
support.text: Pemetrexed rash prevention uses dexamethasone-equivalent 4 mg twice daily on the day before, day of and day after treatment. The anti-sickness plan also uses steroids. Your prescriber/pharmacist must provide one reconciled schedule; do not add two courses together.

support.title: Preventing and treating sickness
support.text: This cisplatin combination has high sickness risk. Take prevention medicines as prescribed even when you feel well, and keep the team’s rescue plan available. The usual high-risk reference includes olanzapine; ask about sleepiness, falls and interactions.

support.title: Fluids and kidney protection
support.text: Ask for an individual drinking plan, especially with heart or kidney problems. Report inability to drink or reduced urine. Cisplatin needs supervised fluids before and after treatment; additional salts may be prescribed.

support.title: Medicines and self-care
support.text: Check all prescriptions, painkillers, supplements and vaccines with the oncology team. Some anti-inflammatory medicines can affect pemetrexed clearance; do not start or stop them on this guide’s authority. Follow mouth-care and infection advice.

evidence.title: Evidence depends on the cancer and the exact medicines
evidence.intro: Ask which study and treatment aim match your situation.
evidence.population: Pleural mesothelioma and advanced NSCLC were studied in different trials.
evidence.interpretation: In unresectable pleural mesothelioma, a randomised study found better survival with pemetrexed plus cisplatin than cisplatin alone. A different advanced NSCLC trial compared cisplatin/pemetrexed with cisplatin/gemcitabine; benefit differed by tumour histology, supporting non-squamous selection. These studies cannot predict an individual outcome, and neither describes standalone neoadjuvant immunotherapy.

chronology_notes.title: Before starting
chronology_notes.text: Folate and B12 preparation begins before the first dose; confirm the Day −1 rash steroid.

chronology_notes.title: Day 1 and early days
chronology_notes.text: Both infusions are planned on Day 1. The written anti-sickness schedule extends over the following days; folate continues daily.

chronology_notes.title: No safe-day prediction
chronology_notes.text: Low counts or serious symptoms can occur between visits. The position in the cycle never rules out infection or another urgent problem.

chronology_notes.title: Across the course
chronology_notes.text: Nerve, hearing and kidney effects can accumulate or persist. The number of cycles and any transition to maintenance depend on the indication and consultant review.

The whole visit also includes blood-result review, prevention medicines, preparation and observation.

sections.title: Access for treatment
sections.text: Treatment may use a small cannula or an existing suitable central line. The team chooses access for your veins and treatment plan. There is no routine take-home infusion pump in this regimen; ask for line-care instructions if you have a line.

sections.title: Home medicines
sections.text: Keep your vitamin, steroid, anti-sickness and rescue plans together. Ask the pharmacist to resolve duplicate dexamethasone directions before taking them.

patient.title: Pemetrexed + Carboplatin

agents.name: Pemetrexed
agents.explanation: Pemetrexed blocks several enzymes that use folate to make the building blocks of DNA and RNA. This can slow or stop cancer-cell growth. Healthy cells can also be affected. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce important toxicities and are part of treatment.
agents.watch: Take the prescribed folic acid and attend for B12. Report mouth sores, diarrhoea, a rash, breathlessness or reduced urine; check before taking ibuprofen or other non-prescription medicines.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Skin rash; rarely serious skin reactions

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. The dose is tailored using kidney function because the kidneys clear carboplatin.
agents.watch: Report ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Report infection or unusual bruising/bleeding promptly and describe any symptoms during the infusion.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hearing changes or tinnitus, which can persist
Numbness or tingling, which can persist

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Is immunotherapy part of these two medicines?
questions.a: This guide covers pemetrexed and carboplatin chemotherapy. It does not include an immunotherapy medicine. If nivolumab, pembrolizumab or another medicine is also prescribed, obtain its separate regimen, consent, monitoring and emergency instructions. Mesothelioma and NSCLC have different aims and evidence; ask which indication is on your prescription.

questions.q: Will I always have four cycles?
questions.a: For pleural mesothelioma, the source describes up to 4–6 cycles. For advanced non-squamous NSCLC, it describes 4–6 combination cycles followed, when appropriate, by a separate pemetrexed maintenance plan (NCCP00222). The selected preoperative nivolumab combination uses three cycles and a separate immunotherapy plan (NCCP00849). Your team confirms which course applies and may stop or change it earlier.

questions.q: Why take vitamins during chemotherapy?
questions.a: Folic acid and vitamin B12 lower important pemetrexed side effects. They are prescribed parts of this regimen. Tell the team promptly if they were missed.

questions.q: What happens when the platinum chemotherapy stops?
questions.a: The next step depends on your disease and treatment aim. Selected advanced NSCLC plans may move to pemetrexed maintenance under a separate regimen. Preoperative treatment leads to a surgical-team review; mesothelioma follow-up is agreed with the oncology team.

patient.timeline_note: This is one reference cycle, not a prediction of when side effects will happen. Risks overlap and symptoms can persist after the last dose.
patient.safety_note: There are no guaranteed safe days. Follow the temperature threshold and emergency instructions given by your unit. Sudden illness, shaking chills or feeling very unwell need urgent advice even without a high temperature.
patient.teachback: Can you describe which two chemotherapy medicines you are receiving, when to take folic acid and steroids, when your B12 injection is due, and which number to call at any hour?
patient.consent_support: Confirm the treatment aim and indication, likely benefit and uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, serious and lasting risks, kidney/hearing/nerve problems, fertility and pregnancy advice, vitamin and steroid plans, and the chance of delays or dose changes. For mesothelioma and advanced NSCLC, the source identifies this carboplatin combination as off-label in Ireland; ask the team to explain this and document consent under hospital policy.
patient.urgent_extra: Call urgently for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, severe or persistent diarrhoea, inability to drink, very little urine, a spreading or blistering rash, or swelling/wheeze during an infusion. Tell the team promptly about new tinnitus, hearing change, numbness, weakness or difficulty walking.
